citation:
CAROLWOOD 707 I, LLC, a California limited

MULTACOM CORPORATION, a California
corporation; and DOES 1 through 20, inclusive,

(26STCV11606, SUPERIOR COURT OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA
IN AND FOR THE COUNTY OF LOS ANGELES)
summary: Carolwood 707 I, LLC and Carolwood 707 II, LLC, owners of the Aon Center office tower at 707 Wilshire Boulevard in Los Angeles, sued their commercial tenant Multacom Corporation for breach of a 2006 office lease (as amended in 2014) covering space used for co-location, data hosting, and networking operations. Plaintiffs allege Multacom defaulted on rent, additional rent, utility charges, and common-area-maintenance and tax obligations totaling at least $401,128.25 as of April 1, 2026, following an earlier, related suit (Case No. 25STCV11338) in which Multacom had also defaulted before resuming payment. Plaintiffs seek damages for the unpaid amounts, a declaration that the lease remains in full force through its 2033 term without any rent offset for Multacom's disputed claims about electrical service capacity, and attorneys' fees.

shortName: Hoosier Environmental Council, Inc. v. Indianapolis Metropolitan Development Comm'n
citation: Hoosier Environmental Council, Inc., Joyce A McReynolds, a/k/a Joyce Redeemar, Cierra Johnsonet al vs. Indianapolis Metropolitan Development Commission, Metrobloks, LLC, Sherman Investments LLC
summary: The Hoosier Environmental Council, joined by several residents of Indianapolis's historically Black Martindale-Brightwood neighborhood, filed a petition for judicial review challenging the Indianapolis Metropolitan Development Commission's April 1, 2026 approval of zoning variances allowing developer Metrobloks (based in Los Angeles) to build a roughly $500 million, 75-megawatt data center on a 14-acre site near 25th Street and Sherman Drive. Petitioners argue the approval failed to adequately consider potential environmental harms — including noise and air-quality impacts — in a community that has historically borne disproportionate industrial pollution burdens, including prior lead contamination, and frame the project as continuing a pattern of environmental injustice; they seek to have the rezoning approval overturned and construction halted.

shortName: Sierra Club v. Town of Torrey
citation: Matter of Sierra Club v. Town of Torrey
summary: The Sierra Club, Seneca Lake Guardian, the Committee to Preserve the Finger Lakes, and more than 20 individual residents filed an Article 78 petition against the Town of Torrey, its Planning Board, and Greenidge Generation LLC, challenging the town's approval of a site plan expanding Bitcoin-mining data center operations at the Greenidge natural-gas power plant on Seneca Lake. Petitioners alleged Greenidge improperly split its regulatory approvals into "two separate but interdependent" applications to evade full review, and that the increased power generation needed to run the expanded mining operation continuously would increase harmful warm-water discharges into Seneca Lake, harming fish populations, increasing algae blooms, and interfering with boating and swimming. This litigation is related to, but distinct from, Greenidge's separate dispute with the state Department of Environmental Conservation over renewal of its Title V air permit (summarized in an earlier batch), which was ultimately resolved through a 2025 settlement.

shortName: Ashland Hospital Corp. v. Affiliated FM Insurance Co.
citation: Ashland Hospital Corporation v. Affiliated FM Insurance Company
summary: Ashland Hospital Corporation (d/b/a King's Daughters Medical Center) sued its property insurer, Affiliated FM Insurance Company, in federal court after an air-conditioning failure in the hospital's data storage facility in March 2010 caused overheating that rendered patient records and scheduling systems unavailable for several hours. The hospital replaced the damaged data storage unit (a EMC "DMX-4") with a newer system and sought insurance coverage for the replacement; Affiliated FM denied the claim, disputing whether the replacement equipment was "of like kind and quality" as required under the policy. In a June 24, 2013 Memorandum Opinion and Order, the court ruled on an evidentiary motion excluding the insurer's expert opinion testimony ahead of further proceedings on the coverage dispute.

shortName: Pacheco v. Bd. of Cnty. Comm'rs of Dona Ana Cnty.
citation: Derrick Pacheco vs. Board of County Commissioners of Dona Ana County
corporateEntities: Project Jupiter; BorderPlex Digital Assets; Oracle; Open AI; Yucca Growth Infrastructure; Green Chile Ventures, LLC
summary: Las Cruces resident Derrick Pacheco sued the Doña Ana County Board of County Commissioners, alleging the county acted improperly when it approved the "Project Jupiter" data center campus — backed by BorderPlex Digital Assets and involving proposed natural-gas "microgrids" — even though the project had not yet gone through the county's Planning and Zoning Commission review process. This is one of several related lawsuits challenging Project Jupiter's approval; the county has moved to dismiss both this case and a separate, related suit alleging the county board voted on an incomplete application when it approved $165 billion in government-backed bonds for the project.

shortName: In re Interconnection & Tariffs for Large Load Customers
citation: In re: Interconnection and Tariffs for Large Load Customers
summary: This is a Commission-initiated rulemaking rather than adversarial litigation. The Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission (PUC) opened a proceeding to develop statewide guidance for how electric utilities should interconnect and set tariff terms for large-load customers, including data centers, amid a surge in electricity-demand requests tied to AI and advanced manufacturing. On May 13, 2026, the PUC issued a final, nonbinding order establishing what it called a "first-of-its-kind" model tariff framework, recommending that utilities charge large-load customers (over 50 MW individually or 100 MW in aggregate) for grid upgrades that would not have been needed "but for" their interconnection — including through upfront "Contributions in Aid of Construction" payments — while also setting guidance on collateral requirements, six-month interconnection-study timelines, minimum contract terms, and public disclosure of large-load interconnection requests.

shortName: Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing, LLC vs. Imperial Irrigation District
citation: Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing, LLC vs. Imperial Irrigation District
summary: Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing (IVCM) sued the Imperial Irrigation District (IID) after IID denied IVCM's April 22, 2026 application for industrial water service, seeking roughly 260–287 million gallons (about 880 acre-feet) of Colorado River water annually to cool its proposed 330-megawatt AI data center. IVCM alleges IID broke its own rules by denying an industrial applicant the right to combine water rights from contiguous, commonly-owned parcels — a "farm unit" consolidation IID routinely permits for agricultural users — and contends there is "no rational basis" for IID to treat industrial and agricultural water-reallocation requests differently. IVCM describes the request as a "last resort" after months of failed negotiations for recycled wastewater with the cities of El Centro and Imperial, and says the request represents a small fraction (roughly 0.03%) of IID's total Colorado River allocation; the suit asks the court to order IID to reconsider or approve the water-service application.

shortName: Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing, LLC v. City of Imperial
citation: Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing, LLC v. City of Imperial et al
summary: Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing, LLC (developer of the proposed $10 billion Imperial Valley AI data center) filed a federal civil-rights lawsuit against the City of Imperial and four named officials (a city council member, the city manager, the city attorney, and the planning director), alleging a coordinated campaign of "administrative obstruction" and retaliation that derailed the project after it was originally proposed on city-zoned land. The developer alleges the city failed to act on three successive site plans within the 15-day period required by city code (after which plans are "deemed approved" by law), prompting the developer to relocate the project to a county-zoned parcel — after which the city sued Imperial County to block that separate approval (the CEQA-based dispute summarized in an earlier batch, Case ID 6). The complaint also alleges a conspiracy between city officials and the Imperial Irrigation District to favor other, unrelated energy projects, and that a city councilmember coordinated with outside groups to use environmental litigation as a pretext to stall the project; the developer seeks damages and has offered to drop claims against the city itself if individual officials personally cover their own legal defense costs.

shortName: McNerney,  et al. v. City of Fort Meade
citation: McNerney,  et al. v. City of Fort Meade
summary: George McNerney and four other Fort Meade, Florida residents — organized as the "Watchdogs of Fort Meade" — filed two lawsuits on May 14, 2026 against the City of Fort Meade after its City Commission voted 5-0 on April 14, 2026 to approve a 20-year development agreement for a $2.6 billion, 4.4-million-square-foot Stonebridge hyperscale AI data center campus on a 1,300-acre former phosphate mine, despite 40 of 41 public commenters speaking in opposition. One suit, a petition for writ of certiorari, alleges the city failed to properly notify residents of key hearings held in 2025 and never adequately reviewed whether the project was compatible with the surrounding neighborhood before approval; the Florida Department of Commerce separately called the city's review "fundamentally flawed" and criticized the developer's water-demand estimates as significantly understated. Plaintiffs ask the court to void the city's approval; they have also launched a recall campaign against three city commissioners.

shortName: Greene et al. v. Nebius Inc. et al
citation: Greene et al. v. Nebius Inc. et al
summary: Birmingham, Alabama residents Madelyn Greene and David Butler filed a class-action lawsuit against Nebius and the City of Birmingham over the proposed "Birmingham AI Factory," a 300-megawatt AI data center campus near Oxmoor Valley. Plaintiffs allege the city allowed the project to proceed without required zoning approvals or public hearings, contending the site's mixed-use zoning does not permit a hyperscale facility and that any "grandfathered" development rights tied to a prior building on the site were lost when that building was demolished. The suit further challenges the adequacy of approval for a proposed power substation and switching station — which failed to receive enough votes from the city's Zoning Board of Adjustment in March 2026 — and an internal city attorney memo the plaintiffs say improperly tried to override that board's action; plaintiffs seek to halt construction and recover damages for property values and quality of life.

shortName: MCEA v. City of North Mankato
citation: MCEA v. City of North Mankato
summary: The Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy sued the City of North Mankato in August 2025, alleging the city's Alternative Urban Areawide Review (AUAR) for privately owned land in nearby Belgrade Township — funded by Project Deacon LLC and evaluating a "technology park" or office/warehouse scenario — was conducted without adequate transparency about a suspected data center project, based on internal city records MCEA obtained through a public records request. After the lawsuit was filed, the city informed MCEA that although two companies had considered a data center at the site, neither had advanced an actual proposal; MCEA voluntarily dismissed the suit without prejudice in May 2026, meaning the dismissal did not resolve the merits and MCEA could refile if a concrete project later emerges. The city maintains the dismissal validates its handling of the environmental review.

shortName: Clean Wisconsin v. FERC
citation: Clean Wisconsin v. FERC
summary: Clean Wisconsin, joined by the Natural Resources Defense Council and Sierra Club (represented by Earthjustice), petitioned for review of a Federal Energy Regulatory Commission order approving the Midcontinent Independent System Operator's (MISO) Expedited Resource Addition Study (ERAS) process, which fast-tracks grid interconnection for certain — mostly fossil-fueled — generation projects, including new gas plants intended to serve data centers. Petitioners argue FERC's approval improperly allows fast-tracked projects to shift significant grid-upgrade costs onto residential customers and to jump ahead of thousands of megawatts of cheaper clean-energy projects that have been waiting years in MISO's normal interconnection queue, in violation of FERC's mandate to ensure just and reasonable rates.

shortName: LBT Investment Group LLC v. Sugarloaf Twp. Bd. of Supervisors
citation: LBT Investment Group LLC v. Sugarloaf Township Board Of Supervisors
summary: LBT Investment Group, a Chicago-based developer, filed a curative-amendment land use appeal against Sugarloaf Township, Pennsylvania after the township's Board of Supervisors denied LBT's request to build a data center, arguing the township's zoning ordinance was legally defective because it failed to provide for data center use anywhere in the township — a use Pennsylvania law requires municipalities to accommodate somewhere within their zoning map. While the appeal has been pending, LBT and the township have been negotiating a proposed ordinance amendment to regulate data centers (which LBT says would use a closed-loop cooling system withdrawing roughly 100,000 gallons per building, comparable to an already-approved warehouse on the same site), though the township tabled a vote on the draft ordinance in February 2026 amid resident opposition and a separate challenge by resident counsel to LBT's standing to pursue the appeal, based on questions about whether LBT is properly registered to do business in Pennsylvania.

shortName: Cook v. City of Villa Rica
citation: Cook v. City of Villa Rica, the Embry Development Company
summary: This case appears to concern the "Avemore" data center project in Villa Rica, Georgia — originally proposed as residential and senior-living development before being reoriented toward data center use by Atlas Development after the city council voted 4-1 in January 2025 to approve a technology park overlay district, which was followed by a rezoning and annexation request. Available secondary sources describe broad regional opposition to data center development (citing environmental impact, water usage, and power consumption concerns) but do not detail the specific allegations, legal theories, or relief sought in this particular filing.

shortName: In re Application for Approval of Generation & Transmission Resources (Project in North Louisiana)
citation:
In Re: Application for Approval of Generation and Transmission Resources in Connection with Service to a Single Customer for a
Project in North Louisiana
summary: Entergy Louisiana applied to the Louisiana Public Service Commission for approval to build three new gas-fired power plants, at a cost exceeding $3 billion, to supply electricity to Meta's roughly 4-million-square-foot, 2+ gigawatt AI data center campus ("Project Evest"/Hyperion) in Richland Parish — a facility Meta has described as one of its largest. The Alliance for Affordable Energy and other consumer and environmental advocacy groups, which intervened in the proceeding, sought to compel Meta and its subsidiary Laidley LLC to join as parties, arguing that key information about the project's promised jobs, sustainability commitments, and claimed urgency for power was missing from Entergy's application and that ratepayers could ultimately bear costs associated with the decades-long gas plants. On April 4, 2025, an administrative law judge denied that request, ruling the Commission had adequate tools (such as subpoenas and depositions) to obtain needed information without requiring Meta's formal participation; the underlying application for the generation resources remains pending before the full Commission.

shortName: Metropolitan Milwaukee Association of Commerce, Inc. v. City of Port Washington
citation: Metropolitan Milwaukee Association of Commerce, Inc. et al v. City of Port Washington et al
corporateEntities: Vantage Data Center "Lighthouse"; Open AI; Oracle
summary: The Metropolitan Milwaukee Association of Commerce (MMAC), joined by six other business and trade groups, sued the City of Port Washington and its city clerk, challenging the legality of a proposed ordinance — placed on the April 2026 ballot after a citizens' petition (organized by Great Lakes Neighbors United in response to the $458 million tax incremental district approved for Vantage Data Center's "Lighthouse" campus) — that would require voter referendum approval for any future tax incremental district financing over $10 million. MMAC argued the referendum requirement conflicts with state statutes that already govern the TID approval process and would be economically damaging, and sought an injunction blocking the referendum from taking effect; the referendum passed at the April 7, 2026 election regardless, and a court dismissed MMAC's suit, though MMAC has indicated it plans to appeal.

shortName: Atlas Industrial Contractors LLC v. In2Gro Technologies LLC
citation: Atlas Industrial Contractors LLC v. In2Gro Technologies LLC
summary: Atlas Industrial Contractors sued In2Gro Technologies in federal court for breach of contract and unjust enrichment, alleging In2Gro failed to pay approximately $177,686.50 for "standby" and other work Atlas performed as a subcontractor on security systems for an Amazon Web Services data center in New Albany, Ohio. Atlas had also filed (and later released) a mechanics lien on the AWS facility for a larger sum representing its total claimed unpaid work. The Southern District of Ohio granted Atlas partial summary judgment, awarding it $177,686.50; In2Gro appealed the judgment to the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals in April 2021.

shortName: Maryland Office of People's Counsel v. PJM Interconnection, LLC
citation: Maryland Office of People’s Counsel v. PJM Interconnection, LLC
summary: The Maryland Office of People's Counsel (OPC), which represents Maryland utility ratepayers, filed a complaint with FERC on May 7, 2026 alleging that PJM Interconnection's "hybrid" methodology for allocating the costs of regional high-voltage transmission projects violates the Federal Power Act by unfairly shifting data-center-driven infrastructure costs onto Maryland customers. OPC's complaint, supported by an expert affidavit, alleges that of $22 billion in transmission project costs PJM has advanced over the past three years — overwhelmingly to meet data center demand concentrated in states like Virginia, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Illinois — PJM's rules have assigned Maryland customers (mostly served by Baltimore Gas and Electric and Pepco) roughly $2 billion in capital costs that will add an estimated $1.6 billion to Maryland electric bills over the next decade, despite Maryland's comparatively modest data-center-driven load growth. OPC asks FERC to require PJM to assign data-center-driven transmission costs to the specific PJM zones where the data centers are located, or alternatively to charge those costs directly to the large data center customers themselves, consistent with a "Ratepayer Protection Pledge" signed by hyperscale developers at the White House on March 4, 2026.

shortName: Midwest Environmental Advocates v. Wisconsin Public Service Comm'n
citation: Midwest Environmental Advocates vs. Wisconsin Public Service Commission
summary: Midwest Environmental Advocates, a nonprofit law center, sued the Wisconsin Public Service Commission (PSC) after the agency denied an open-records request seeking unredacted documents showing the expected electrical demand of Meta's data center campus in Beaver Dam, Wisconsin. The group's complaint alleges the PSC "arbitrarily and capriciously" withheld the information by classifying it as a trade secret, even though the PSC had released comparable unredacted electricity-demand data (showing a 1,300-megawatt transmission interconnection request) for a separate data center project in Port Washington; the suit argues electrical-load figures do not meet the legal definition of a trade secret under Wisconsin law because they lack independent economic value. The group seeks a court order compelling the PSC to release the withheld Beaver Dam demand figures.

shortName: Lupia v. Fermi Inc.
citation: Lupia v. Fermi Inc.
summary: Lead plaintiff Salvatore Lupia filed a putative securities class action against Fermi Inc. — an energy and AI infrastructure company planning large-scale nuclear reactors to power its own grid-independent data centers — along with certain of its directors, officers, and IPO underwriters, on behalf of investors who purchased Fermi stock in or traceable to its October 2025 initial public offering (which raised roughly $784 million) or on the open market between October 1 and December 11, 2025. The complaint, centered on Fermi's "Project Matador" data center campus, alleges Fermi's IPO materials and subsequent statements misrepresented the strength of tenant demand for the project by touting a $150 million "Advance in Aid of Construction" agreement with an investment-grade "First Tenant," without adequately disclosing how concentrated and fragile that arrangement was; when Fermi disclosed on December 12, 2025 that the First Tenant had terminated the agreement after its exclusivity period expired, the stock fell roughly 33%. The suit asserts claims under Sections 10(b) and 20(a) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Sections 11 and 15 of the Securities Act of 1933, seeking damages on behalf of the affected investor class.

shortName: FLX Strong v. Town of Lansing Zoning Bd. of Appeals
citation: FLX Strong et al v. Town Of Lansing Zoning Board Of Appeals et al
corporateEntities: TeraWulf, Inc., Lake Hawkeye, LLC; Cuyahoga Operating Co., LLC
summary: FLX Strong and Cayuga Lake Environmental Action Now (CLEAN) filed an Article 78 petition against the Town of Lansing Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA) and developers TeraWulf Inc., its subsidiary Lake Hawkeye LLC, property owner Cayuga Operating Company, and an individual applicant, challenging the ZBA's December 22, 2025 decision (by a 3-2 vote) that a proposed data center at the former Cayuga Power Plant qualifies as a "general processing facility" — a permitted-by-right use under the town's Industrial Research zoning district — rather than requiring a more rigorous review process. Petitioners allege the ZBA's interpretation improperly stretched a legacy industrial zoning category to fit modern data center infrastructure, allowing the project to bypass environmental review, and that the proceedings were tainted by bias (citing the ZBA chairperson's private email expressing hope the project would be approved) and procedural irregularities, including a compressed 12-day review period. The petition asks the court to annul the ZBA's determination and remand for a new hearing excluding the chairperson; the matter was later appealed to the Appellate Division, Third Department.

shortName: Devlin Defend Corp. v. Bd. of Cnty. Supervisors of Prince William Cnty.
citation: Devlin Defend Corporation v. Bd. of Cnty. Supervisors of Prince William Cnty
summary: A group of Prince William County, Virginia residents, organized as the nonprofit "Devlin Defend Corporation," sued the county Board of County Supervisors on December 28, 2023, seeking to overturn the Board's November 29, 2023 approval rezoning roughly 270 acres from "Planned Mixed Residential" to "M-2 Light Industrial" for the nine-building "Devlin Technology Park" data center campus in Bristow. The 473-page suit alleged the rezoning was an "invasive industrial use" that would tower over nearby homes (with structures reaching 81 feet), that developer Stanley Martin Homes was treated more favorably than other applicants, and that the Board violated its own Code of Ordinances and Virginia zoning law — including by declining to send an amended, less-generous version of the developer's proposal back to the Planning Commission for review after the developer withdrew earlier community-benefit commitments. The circuit court sustained demurrers filed by the Board and Stanley Martin Homes, holding the rezoning decision fell within the Board's discretion and that plaintiffs had not stated a valid legal claim; the Virginia Court of Appeals affirmed this outcome on September 16, 2025 in a related case brought by overlapping plaintiffs (Caparoula v. Board of County Supervisors), and the property was reportedly later sold to Amazon Data Services.

shortName: Fortes v. Massachusetts Dep't of Environmental Protection
citation: Fortes, Jacob et al vs. Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection et al
summary: Jake Fortes and other residents of the Sacred Heart neighborhood in Lowell, Massachusetts sued the Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) and data center operator the Markley Group, appealing DEP's approval of an air permit allowing Markley to add up to eight additional diesel backup generators (bringing the facility's total to 27) at its more than 350,000-square-foot data center. Plaintiffs allege DEP failed to adequately consider the neighborhood's existing pollution burden before approving the expansion and improperly allowed construction to proceed while their administrative challenge was still pending; residents separately report diesel fumes entering nearby homes when the generators run. On August 10, 2026, a Superior Court judge stayed enforcement of the air permit as to the four generators not yet installed (while allowing four already-installed generators to keep operating under the permit's existing conditions), finding that Markley's community engagement "appears to have been lacking" based on the limited record before the court; the Lowell City Council has separately imposed a 360-day moratorium on further expansion at the site.

shortName: Keep It Rural LLC v. Columbus Council
citation: Keep It Rural LLC et al v. Columbus Council et al
summary: Keep It Rural LLC and eight individual property owners near a proposed 900-acre, $5.18 billion "Project Ruby" data center site in the Upatoi area sued the Columbus, Georgia Council (Mayor Skip Henderson and all ten councilors) over its June 16, 2026 approval of a new data center overlay ordinance. Plaintiffs allege the council violated the Georgia Zoning Procedures Law by amending the ordinance's terms (setbacks, noise rules, and energy-generation policy) after the public hearing and adopting the revised version without further public input, and that an "unofficial committee" vetted the overlay behind closed doors in violation of Georgia's Open Meetings Act; they also allege the overlay amounts to unlawful "spot zoning" designed specifically to enable Project Ruby, since land already zoned for heavy industrial use elsewhere in the county was not used. The suit seeks a temporary restraining order and asks the court to declare the ordinance unconstitutional and void, or alternatively to send the matter back to the council to redo the process lawfully; the city disputes that the overlay itself rezones any property or that any data center application has yet been filed.

shortName: In re Archer Datacenters Environmental Assessment Worksheet
citation: In re Archer Datacenters Environmental Assessment Worksheet
summary: The Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy (MCEA) appealed the City of Faribault's August 2025 decision — following review of an Environmental Assessment Worksheet (EAW) — that a more rigorous Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) was not required for Archer Datacenter's proposed 500,000-square-foot, six-building data center campus. MCEA alleges the city's EAW "vastly underreported" the project's likely impact on climate change and Minnesota's electricity grid, pointing to an unexplained 98% drop in the facility's estimated annual greenhouse-gas emissions (tied to a reported electricity-use estimate that fell from over 1 million to just 14,000 megawatt-hours per year) between the draft and final versions of the study, and argues the EAW failed to analyze the cumulative impact of the wave of data centers proposed in nearby Minnesota communities or to address residents' concerns. This was the third of several MCEA appeals challenging Minnesota cities' environmental reviews of proposed data centers.

shortName: International Transmission Co. v. Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.
citation: Grid Acceleration Coal. v. Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc.
summary: A coalition of electric utilities calling itself the "Grid Acceleration Coalition" — including Xcel Energy and American Transmission Company — filed a complaint with FERC on April 7, 2026 asking the agency to pause or exempt certain transmission projects from MISO's competitive-bidding process, arguing that bidding-related delays are slowing the grid buildout needed to meet surging data center electricity demand and could jeopardize U.S. competitiveness in AI development. The coalition proposed either letting MISO exempt projects case-by-case or suspending competitive bidding entirely for five years. Ratepayer advocacy groups and a rival industry coalition oppose the complaint, arguing competitively bid projects have a comparable or better record of meeting cost and schedule targets than non-competitive ones, and that suspending competition would raise costs for ordinary electricity customers.

shortName: Joliet Residents for Responsible Growth v. City of Joliet
citation: Joliet Residents for Responsible Growth v. City of Joliet
corporateEntities: Powerhouse Hillwood Holding, LLC; HW Technology Park Development, LLC; American Real Estate Partners; City of Joliet.
summary: Joliet Residents for Responsible Growth, along with three individual plaintiffs living near the proposed site, sued the City of Joliet and developers Powerhouse Hillwood Holding, HW Technology Park Development, and American Real Estate Partners, challenging the City Council's March 19, 2026 approval (by an 8-1 vote) of an annexation agreement for the $20 billion, 795-acre "Joliet Technology Center" data center campus. The suit alleges the city's February 18 public notice for the Plan Commission hearing failed to disclose that the project involved a 24-building, 1.8-gigawatt data center as required by Illinois law; that a March 19 special council meeting violated the Open Meetings Act by not occurring within 24 hours of a prior meeting with an unchanged agenda; that residents were denied due process, including the right to cross-examine developer witnesses; and that rezoning the land from agricultural to light industrial is unconstitutional because it bears no substantial relation to public health, safety, or welfare. The suit also alleges a conflict of interest because the city's planning director is the daughter of a person with a financial stake in the project, and asks the court to void the City Council's approval.

citation: McNerney,  et al. v. City of Fort Meade
summary: George McNerney and four other Fort Meade, Florida residents — organized as the "Watchdogs of Fort Meade" — filed two lawsuits on May 14, 2026 against the City of Fort Meade after its City Commission voted 5-0 on April 14, 2026 to approve a 20-year development agreement for a $2.6 billion, 4.4-million-square-foot Stonebridge hyperscale AI data center campus on a 1,300-acre former phosphate mine, despite 40 of 41 public commenters speaking in opposition. One suit, a petition for writ of certiorari, alleges the city failed to properly notify residents of key hearings held in 2025 and never adequately reviewed whether the project was compatible with the surrounding neighborhood before approval; the Florida Department of Commerce separately called the city's review "fundamentally flawed" and criticized the developer's water-demand estimates as significantly understated. shortName: Coalition for Responsible Data Center Development v. City of Farmington
citation: Coalition for Responsible Data Center Development et al., v. City of Farmington, Minnesota
corporateEntities: Tract; MNLCO Farmington LLC; MNLCO Farmington Two LLC
summary: The Coalition for Responsible Data Center Development, a group of more than 350 residents, along with individual Farmington homeowners, sued the City of Farmington after its council approved a final plat and planned-unit development allowing developer Tract (through MNLCO Farmington LLC and MNLCO Farmington Two LLC) to build up to 12 data center buildings across 340 acres. Plaintiffs allege the city was barred from rezoning the parcels without the consent of neighboring Castle Rock Township under a pre-existing Orderly Annexation Agreement, and that the project will harm residents' physical and mental wellbeing through worsened air quality, noise, and "unprecedented" water and electricity use. They sought to invalidate the city's approvals and halt construction.

shortName: Bryan v. Pioneer Development LLC
citation: John Bryan v. Pioneer Development LLC
summary: Yorkville, Illinois resident John Bryan sued the City of Yorkville (with developer Pioneer Development LLC later joining as a defendant) on October 28, 2025 to halt the roughly 1,037-acre "Project Cardinal" data center campus — planned as 14 two-story buildings to be constructed over a decade or more — arguing the project and its lengthy construction period would negatively impact his property values and quality of life, including through noise pollution not accounted for in a sound study the developers had commissioned (which did not address noise from the 10- to 20-year construction period). The City approved the project's annexation, rezoning, and utility and infrastructure agreements in March 2026 notwithstanding the pending suit; the parties reported "substantial progress" toward a settlement at a March 20, 2026 hearing, with the final terms subject to Yorkville City Council approval.

shortName: Curtis v. City of Sulphur Springs
citation: Jack Curtis v. City of Sulphur Springs, Texas, et al.
summary: Sulphur Springs, Texas resident Jack Curtis sued the City of Sulphur Springs, alleging the city violated the Texas Open Meetings Act in connection with its dealings with MSB Global, the developer behind a proposed large AI data center project in the city. Curtis contends that City Council meeting minutes and agendas lacked sufficient detail about a letter of intent (LOI) between the city and MSB Global — including failing to name MSB Global as the counterparty — depriving the public of a meaningful opportunity to know what was being negotiated; the suit asks the court to declare the resulting agreements between the city and MSB Global void. This is a separate lawsuit from an earlier suit brought by former landowner Vistra Corp. and its subsidiary Luminant Mining, which alleges the city violated a deed restriction from Vistra's 2019 bankruptcy-related land donation that bars energy production or storage on the site (summarized in an earlier batch as City of Sulphur Springs v. Luminant Mining Co.).

shortName: In re Lee Cnty. Generating Station, LLC
citation: Lee County Generating Station, LLC; Tait Electric Generating Station, LLC; Hull Street Energy, LLC; GridFlex Generation, LLC
summary: Hull Street Energy (HSE) and Rockland Capital filed an application with FERC under Section 203 of the Federal Power Act seeking approval for HSE to acquire two gas-fired power plants from Rockland — the 677-megawatt Lee County generating station in Dixon, Illinois, and the 590-megawatt Tait generating station near Dayton, Ohio — together totaling roughly 1,267 megawatts. PJM's independent market monitor, Monitoring Analytics, filed opposition with FERC on April 24, 2026, arguing the deal should be rejected or conditioned because HSE — which is separately redeveloping the retired Sammis power plant site in Ohio into an energy and data center campus — could redirect the acquired plants away from PJM's wholesale capacity market to serve data centers directly, shifting the cost and reliability risk of that load onto other PJM customers and enhancing HSE's ability to exercise market power. The market monitor asked FERC to require HSE and Rockland to refile with a commitment not to remove the plants from the PJM market to serve data centers; this is one of several similar market monitor challenges to power-plant sales tied to data center developers.

shortName: Data Foundry, Inc. v. City of Austin
citation: Data Foundry, Inc. v. City of Austin
summary: Data Foundry, Inc., an internet service provider operating data centers in Austin, sued the City of Austin over rates charged by Austin Energy, the city-owned electric utility, alleging the rates are unjust, unreasonable, excessive, confiscatory, discriminatory, and constitute a taking. The trial court dismissed Data Foundry's claims for lack of standing; the Fourteenth Court of Appeals held Data Foundry had standing but still affirmed dismissal of the claims on other grounds. On April 9, 2021, the Texas Supreme Court held that Data Foundry has standing as a ratepayer to challenge generally applicable municipal utility rates without needing to show an injury distinct from other ratepayers, reversed the courts below in part, and remanded the case to the trial court for further proceedings on the merits of the rate challenge.

shortName: Sardo v. Archbald Borough Council
citation: Sardo, et al. v. Archbald Borough Council

shortName: Gonzalez v. Holland
citation: Gonzalez v. Holland
summary: Rachel Gonzalez and other Independence, Missouri residents sued the city after it rejected their referendum petition seeking to place the city council's more than $6 billion, 20-year, 90% tax-incentive package for a Nebius "AI factory" data center on the ballot. The city argued its charter did not permit a referendum because the ordinance granting the incentives had already taken effect, while plaintiffs contended the charter allowed a public vote and the ordinance could not take effect until the referendum process concluded. On March 25, 2026, a Jackson County judge ruled in the city's favor, holding residents could not force a public vote on the tax breaks.

shortName: City of The Dalles v. Oregonian Publishing Co.
citation: City of The Dalles v. Oregonian Publ’g Co
summary: The City of The Dalles filed a "reverse" public-records lawsuit against The Oregonian and reporter Mike Rogoway after the Wasco County District Attorney ordered the city to disclose Google's water-usage records at its local data centers, which the city (at Google's request and with Google covering its legal fees) argued were protected trade secrets under Oregon's public records law. The Oregonian, represented by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, argued the water-use data did not qualify as a trade secret and that the public had a right to the information. After roughly 13 months of litigation, the city dropped the suit and settled in December 2022, agreeing to release 10 years of Google's water-use data and to disclose the figures annually going forward; the city also paid The Oregonian's attorney fees, which Google reimbursed.

shortName: National CRE Holdings LLC, et al. v. Hood Cty. Texas, et al.
citation: National CRE Holdings LLC, et al. v. Hood Cty. Texas, et al.
corporateEntities: National CRE Holdings and Greenland Capital

shortName: Preserve Our Yorkville & Community, LLC v. City of Yorkville
citation: Preserve Our Yorkville & Community, LLC, Lorie Teska, Patti Bakala, Joan McArthur, PB's Pup Palace, Maplehurst Farm Racing, and Maplehurst Veterinary Services v. The City of Yorkville, Illinois

shortName: State ex rel. Snyder v. City of Joplin
citation: State of Mo. Ex rel. Derk A. & Laura J. Snyder, Teustees, et al. v. City of Joplin, MO, et al.

shortName: Greater Indiantown Community Alliance Inc. v. Florida Power & Light Co.
citation: Greater Indiantown Community Alliance et al. v. Village of Indiantown
summary: The Greater Indiantown Community Alliance and four Martin County property owners sued over the Village of Indiantown's April 30, 2026 approval of the Tesoro Groves Planned Unit Development, which rezoned more than 5,700 acres of farmland — purchased by Florida Power & Light Company — to light industrial use. The complaint raises four claims under Florida land-use law: that the rezoning constitutes illegal spot zoning; that it creates an illegal land enclave; that it conflicts with the Village's Comprehensive Plan and rural character; and that the Village granted final approval before completing a cumulative aquifer-impact analysis that the Village's own staff had determined was necessary.

shortName: MCEA v. City of Monticello
citation: MCEA v. City of Monticello; Monticello Tech, LLC
summary: The Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy (MCEA) sued the City of Monticello and developer Monticello Tech LLC, challenging the city's approval of an Alternative Urban Areawide Review (AUAR) for a roughly 550-acre industrial area where a large-scale technology campus could be developed. MCEA alleges the AUAR — which estimated the potential development could use 250 to 300 million gallons of water annually along with significant electricity demand — did not meet the environmental review requirements of Minnesota law, and asks the court to require more rigorous review, potentially including a full Environmental Impact Statement. The city and developer have denied the claims, arguing the AUAR was comparable in rigor to a full EIS and that MCEA lacks standing; the case is proceeding through discovery toward summary judgment, and the city has separately adopted a Data Center Planned Unit Development ordinance establishing zoning standards for any future proposals.

shortName: In re Consumers Energy Co.
citation: In the Matter of the Application of Consumers Energy Company for Ex Parte Approval of Certain Amendments to Rate GPD
summary: This is a regulatory rate proceeding rather than adversarial litigation. Consumers Energy applied to the Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC) in February 2025, initially seeking expedited ("ex parte") approval, to amend its General Primary Demand Rate (Rate GPD) tariff to add specific terms for data centers and other very large electricity customers (loads of 100 megawatts or more, or aggregated loads meeting that threshold under common ownership). After several parties objected to ex parte treatment, the MPSC opened a contested case with formal hearings involving the Michigan Attorney General, data center industry representatives, environmental groups, and industrial-customer associations. On November 6, 2025, the MPSC approved Consumers Energy's amended tariff terms, including a minimum 15-year contract term, a minimum monthly billing demand of 80% of expected use regardless of actual consumption, and a ramp-up period of up to five years, intended to prevent other ratepayers from subsidizing the costs or risks of serving large data center loads.

shortName: In re Griffin
citation: In re Pamela Griffin, Jose Orta, Carrie D'Anna, and Sarah Winters
summary: This is the appeal of a Williamson County trial court's October 8, 2025 dismissal of a lawsuit brought by five residents living near a proposed 135,000-square-foot Blueprint Data Centers facility in Taylor, Texas. The underlying suit alleged the data center site was subject to a 1999 deed restriction under which the prior owners conveyed the land "to be held in trust for future use as parkland," and sought to block all commercial development on the property, also raising concerns about the project's environmental, health, and safety impacts on the neighborhood. The trial judge dismissed the case for lack of standing and denied a temporary injunction, allowing Blueprint's project (which the company purchased from the city's Economic Development Corporation for $10 million) to proceed; the residents are now pursuing this appeal.

shortName: Young v. Village of Commercial Point
citation: Taise Young, et al. v. Village of Commercial Point

shortName: Minnesota Ctr. for Envir. Advocacy v. City of Lakeville
citation: Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy vs City of Lakeville, Olam Holdings 1, LLC

shortName: Hazelnut LLC v. Town of Groton
citation: Hazelnut LLC v. Town of Groton
summary: 327-449 Hazelnut LLC, owner of a roughly 168-acre parcel on Hazelnut Hill and Flanders Roads in Groton, Connecticut, sued the Town of Groton after its town council voted 5-1 "with prejudice" in March 2022 against entering a host municipality agreement — required under Connecticut law before a data center project can seek local land-use approvals — with developer NE Edge, LLC, which had agreed to purchase the land for $5.25 million to build a data center. The landowner's principal, John Holstein, sought more than $2 million in damages, alleging the town failed to schedule any meeting to discuss NE Edge's proposed community benefits (including annual school payments, donated parkland, and infrastructure extensions), never included NE Edge in negotiations, and failed to consult its own Planning and Zoning Commission on the land's suitability for data center use before rejecting the agreement — actions plaintiff contends significantly reduced the property's value.

shortName: Lansdowne Conservancy v. SCC
citation: Lansdowne Conservancy v. SCC
summary: This is an appeal of a Virginia State Corporation Commission (SCC) order. Dominion Energy applied to the SCC for approval of two new high-voltage transmission lines in eastern Loudoun County — the 9.4-mile "Aspen to Golden" line and the 1.9-mile "Apollo to Twin Creeks" line — which Dominion said were needed to meet growing electricity demand from Northern Virginia data centers. Loudoun County government and the Lansdowne Conservancy had proposed a hybrid alternative burying roughly three miles of the Aspen-to-Golden line along Route 7 to mitigate environmental, viewshed, property-value, and safety concerns near Inova Hospital, commissioning a feasibility study supporting the approach; Dominion disputed the study, estimating undergrounding would cost roughly $1 billion and delay the project. On February 5, 2025, the SCC issued a final order approving both lines as proposed and declining to require undergrounding, finding the hybrid proposal lacked adequate environmental analysis and that the lines were needed and would minimize impacts to the extent reasonably practicable; the Lansdowne Conservancy is now appealing that determination to the Supreme Court of Virginia.

shortName: Cologix COL5, LLC v. 655 Dearborn Park Lane, LLC
citation: Cologix COL5, LLC v. 655 Dearborn Park Lane, LLC
summary: Cologix COL5, LLC sued 655 Dearborn Park Lane, LLC for breach of contract after Cologix agreed in August 2022 to purchase a Columbus, Ohio property from Dearborn to build a data center, then determined during due diligence that it could not obtain sufficient electrical power to the site to support the planned facility and sought to terminate the purchase agreement and recover its earnest money deposit. The district court granted Cologix judgment on the pleadings in March 2024, ordering Dearborn to return the deposit plus interest, fees, and costs; Dearborn appealed to the Sixth Circuit.

shortName: Berkeley Cnty. Council v. Government Properties Income Trust LLC
citation: Berkeley County Council v. Government Properties Income Trust LLC
summary: The Berkeley County Council, sitting as the county Board of Assessment Appeals, appealed circuit court rulings that had reversed the Council's property tax assessments for the 2019 tax year on two commercial properties — one owned by Government Properties Income Trust LLC containing a 30,875-square-foot data center, and a second owned by Martinsburg IRS OC, LLC. The consolidated appeals to the West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals raised, among other issues, whether the county assessor was an indispensable party that should have been named in the taxpayers' original appeals and whether the circuit court erred in its valuation analysis. In a November 10, 2022 opinion, the Supreme Court of Appeals reversed and remanded the circuit court's rulings.

shortName: Stop the Hermantown Data Center v. City of Hermantown
citation: Stop the Hermantown Data Center v. City of Hermantown; Harmony Group, LLC

shortName: Park View Estates Homeowners Association Inc. v. Kipper LLC
citation: Park View Estates Homeowners Association Inc vs. Kipper LLC et al

shortName: MCEA v. City of Hermantown
citation: MCEA; Stop the Hermantown Data Center v. City of Hermantown; Harmony Group, LLC
summary: This entry reflects two related but distinct suits against a proposed roughly $1.2–1.5 billion Google data center campus ("Project Loon") on about 200 acres in Hermantown, Minnesota. The citizens' group Stop the Hermantown Data Center sued the city alleging it improperly amended its 2045 comprehensive plan and rezoned the project site to permit the data center, and that the city violated Minnesota's Open Meeting Law by closing at least three meetings to the public while officials — several of whom had signed non-disclosure agreements — negotiated changes to the development plan with Google. The Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy separately represents the same citizens' group in a companion suit alleging the project's environmental review was legally inadequate, similar to MCEA's suits against other Minnesota cities over data center approvals.

shortName: Minnesota Ctr. for Envir. Advocacy v. City of Pine Island
citation: Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy vs City of Pine Island, Ryan Companies, US, Inc.

shortName: GW Acquisition Co., LLC v. Pageland Limited Liability Co.
citation: GW Acquisition Co., LLC v. Pageland Limited Liability Company
summary: GW Acquisition Co. (an affiliate of QTS Realty Trust) sued landowners Pageland Limited Liability Company and the Mitchell family for breach of contract, alleging they refused to honor purchase-and-sale agreements for roughly 175 acres that were part of GWA's larger, roughly 812-acre "Digital Gateway" data center assemblage in Prince William County, Virginia. GWA alleged the sellers wrongly refused to approve "proffers" needed for GWA's rezoning application and/or sought to terminate the agreements to obtain a higher price, jeopardizing the entire rezoning effort; GWA sought a preliminary injunction and damages, including recovery of legal costs it says it was owed from a related prior dispute with Pageland. The district court found GWA likely to succeed on the merits and that it would suffer irreparable harm without an injunction; Pageland appealed to the Fourth Circuit.

shortName: Applicants Mark and Joan Lippi, et al., Appeal, Tobyhanna Township Board of Supervisors' enactment of Ordinance No. 580
citation: Applicants Mark and Joan Lippi, et al., Appeal, Tobyhanna Township Board of Supervisors' enactment of Ordinance No. 580
summary: Mark and Joan Lippi and several other individuals and a residents' association appealed Tobyhanna Township's December 15, 2025 enactment of Ordinance No. 580, which created a data center overlay district permitting data center use on roughly 520 acres of rural residential land tied to a project by Pennsylvania Glacial Till, LLC. Applicants argue the ordinance constitutes unlawful spot zoning enacted for the exclusive benefit of a single landowner, contradicts the purpose of the township's rural residential zoning district, and is arbitrary and unrelated to public health, safety, or welfare. They ask the Zoning Hearing Board to invalidate the ordinance as unlawful under Pennsylvania municipal zoning law.

shortName: zColo, LLC v. Markley Boston, LLC
citation: zColo, LLC v. Markley Boston, LLC

shortName: Bockrath v. Coweta Cnty.
citation: Bockrath v. Coweta Cnty.
summary: Ron Bockrath and other Coweta County, Georgia residents sued Coweta County over the county commission's approval of rezoning approximately 829 acres near Sargent Road and Wagers Mill Road from Rural Conservation to Industrial use for the proposed "Project Sail" data center campus (13 buildings, roughly 378,000 square feet each). Plaintiffs allege the county violated its own zoning procedures and comprehensive plan by approving industrial development on land designated for rural conservation, that commissioners engaged in improper ex parte communications with the developer, and that the environmental review understated impacts on wetlands and groundwater recharge areas. The petition seeks to void the rezoning decision.

shortName: Land Legacy, Inc. v. Ringle
citation: Land Legacy, Inc. v. Ringle, Alan J.
summary: Land Legacy, Inc., a conservation land trust, sued landowner Alan Ringle and his family, alleging that a 2013 conservation easement covering roughly 270 acres of a larger 800-plus-acre property near Sand Springs, Oklahoma — in exchange for which the Ringles reportedly received a $3.8 million tax deduction — permanently bars industrial development, including roads and buildings, on the land now proposed as the site for a large-scale Google data center ("Project Spring"). Land Legacy alleges the Ringle family knowingly proceeded with the data center plans in bad faith despite the restrictions, and that the easement was not disclosed during the project's rezoning application, which affirmatively denied the existence of any development restrictions on the property; the trust seeks to have the easement enforced and the rezoning process redone with its participation. The City of Sand Springs has stated it does not believe the lawsuit has merit or will affect the project's future.

shortName: In re Iris Energy Ltd. Securities Litigation
citation: In re Iris Energy Limited Securities Litigation
summary: Investors led by Paul Williams-Israel filed a putative class-action securities-fraud lawsuit against Iris Energy Limited (NASDAQ: IREN), a Bitcoin-mining company that had pivoted toward marketing itself as a high-performance computing (HPC) data center operator, and several of its executives. Plaintiffs, representing purchasers of IREN securities between June 20, 2023 and July 11, 2024, allege the company made materially false and misleading statements overstating its Childress County, Texas facility's readiness for HPC workloads — including claims about backup power and cooling infrastructure — based substantially on a July 11, 2024 short-seller report by Culper Research, after which IREN's share price fell roughly 15%. The suit seeks damages under federal securities laws on behalf of the affected investor class; this litigation is separate from an earlier, unrelated 2022 securities suit concerning IREN's 2021 IPO disclosures, which a different judge dismissed without prejudice.

shortName: West Virginia-Citizen Action Group, Inc. v. Crowder
citation: West Virginia-Citizen Action Group, Inc. v. Laura M. Crowder, Director WV DEP
corporateEntities: Microsoft, Nuscale, Fidelis, Monarch Compute Campus

shortName: Hairston Clan v. Stokes Cnty.
citation: Hairston Clan v. Stokes Cnty.
summary: The National Hairston Clan, CleanAIRE NC, the Dan River Basin Association, 7 Directions of Service, and more than a dozen Walnut Cove-area residents sued Stokes County, North Carolina over the county commissioners' January 2026 rezoning votes (approved 3-2) that opened roughly 1,800 acres of land to industrial use for the "Project Delta" hyperscale data center. Plaintiffs allege the rezoning was approved without the procedural safeguards, factual analysis, and reasoned decision-making North Carolina law requires — including inadequate public notice and failure to meaningfully assess impacts on noise, air quality, water, and sites of cultural and historical significance to the Saura Tribe and descendants of formerly enslaved families (including the Hairston and Bailey families) who maintain cemeteries on and near the rezoned land. The suit asks the court to strike down both zoning actions; the county has since voted to restart the rezoning process for the project.

shortName: Independent Market Monitor for PJM v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.
citation: Indep. Mkt. Monitor for PJM v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.
summary: Monitoring Analytics, PJM's independent market monitor (IMM), filed a complaint with FERC on November 25, 2025 raising concerns about the growing impact of data center and other large-load growth on PJM's capacity market, which the IMM's filing states fell short of meeting its reliability objective and reserve-margin target in the most recent capacity auction. The complaint centers on how new large loads — including those that do not commit to bringing their own new generation or agreeing to demand-response curtailment — should be treated for capacity-market purposes, building on the IMM's earlier position (raised in related PJM/FERC proceedings on data center co-location) that new large loads should generally be required to bring their own matching new generation; the complaint asks FERC to address the resulting reliability and cost-allocation risks.

shortName: Clean Air Coalition of Western New York, Inc. v. New York State Public Service Comm'n
citation: Matter of Clean Air Coalition of W. N.Y., Inc. v New York State Pub. Serv. Commn.
summary: The Clean Air Coalition of Western New York and the Sierra Club, represented by Earthjustice, sued the New York State Public Service Commission (PSC) over its approval allowing Digihost International, a Canadian cryptocurrency company, to acquire the Fortistar natural-gas power plant in North Tonawanda for 24/7 crypto-mining operations. Petitioners alleged the PSC failed to analyze the climate and environmental effects of the ownership transfer as required by New York's Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act, contending the plant — which had historically run intermittently for only 10 to 74 days a year — would see its greenhouse gas emissions increase by as much as 3,500% under continuous crypto-mining operation. A trial court initially dismissed the case, but the Appellate Division, Third Department reversed, holding that the petitioners' proximity to the facility gave them standing to challenge the increased use, and returned the case to the trial court to proceed on the merits.

shortName: In re Duke Energy Progress, LLC
citation: In the Matter of: Duke Energy Progress, LLC, and Duke Energy Carolinas, LLC, 2026 Solar Resource Procurement Request for Proposals for Solar and Solar
summary: This proceeding concerns Duke Energy's annual competitive-bidding process for new solar and solar-plus-storage generation, required under North Carolina's 2021 clean-energy law, in a docket where Duke had proposed procuring 770 megawatts of solar for 2026 — short of the 1.7 gigawatts called for under its 2024 regulator-approved carbon-reduction plan, citing federal tax-credit changes. On April 23, 2026, North Carolina Utilities Commission Chair William Brawley issued an order (signed only by the Commission's chief clerk, without an apparent vote of the full panel) deferring Duke's 2026 solar and storage procurement entirely until the company's next carbon-reduction plan is approved by year-end. Clean-energy advocacy groups — including the Sierra Club, Southern Alliance for Clean Energy, and Vote Solar, represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center, along with the Carolinas Clean Energy Business Association — filed motions for reconsideration arguing the order was "arbitrary and capricious," issued without proper Commission process, and would create a solar generation shortfall in the early 2030s just as Duke projects steep demand growth from data centers.

shortName: Haley v. X.AI Corp.
citation: Haley v. X.AI Corp.
summary: Jason Haley, Preston Herrington, and Taylor Logsdon filed a putative class-action lawsuit — on behalf of a class potentially including more than 10,000 residents of Southaven and Horn Lake, Mississippi — against X.AI Corp., SpaceX, and subsidiary MZX Tech, alleging that gas-fired turbines powering xAI's "Colossus" AI data center campus (which grew from roughly 3 to 57 turbines in under a year) create a public and private nuisance through near-constant roaring, humming, and low-frequency vibrations audible and felt in nearby homes 24 hours a day. Plaintiffs assert claims for private nuisance, public nuisance, negligence, negligence per se, and negligent infliction of emotional distress, and seek damages for loss of use and enjoyment of property, diminished property values, and emotional distress, as well as injunctive relief requiring the defendants to abate the noise.

shortName: BCB Cheyenne LLC v. MineOne Wyoming Data Center LLC
citation: BCB Cheyenne LLC v. MineOne Wyoming Data Center LLC
summary: BCB Cheyenne LLC (d/b/a Bison Blockchain) sued MineOne Wyoming Data Center LLC and several related entities (including MineOne Partners, Terra Crypto, SonicHash, and Bit Origin) in federal court, alleging breach of contract, anticipatory repudiation, tortious interference with contractual relations, and related claims arising from a 2022 partnership to develop the North Range and Campstool Bitcoin mining/data center sites near Cheyenne. BCB alleges MineOne pushed it out as operator of both projects without cause and denied it the financial return from the ventures; defendants answered and asserted counterclaims against BCB. The case was terminated in the district court on October 15, 2024 and was subsequently appealed to the Tenth Circuit.

shortName: Rizzo v. Verizon CCC LLC
citation: Rizzo v. Verizon CCC LLC

shortName: Lingelbach v. Twiggs Cnty. Bd. of Comm'rs
citation: Lingelbach v. Twiggs County Board of Commissioners
summary: Twiggs County, Georgia resident Nancy Lingelbach and other residents (including plaintiff and attorney Rob Fricks) sued the Twiggs County Board of Commissioners over its mid-September 2025 approval of a roughly 300-acre data center project proposed by Eagle Rock Partners. Plaintiffs allege the rezoning public notice was improperly posted at the wrong location and that the process was rushed through to bypass Georgia's Development of Regional Impact (DRI) review — a state communication mechanism (not a regulatory approval tool) that was administratively paused at the time — meaning the project's specific square footage and water needs were never disclosed through that review as they otherwise would have been. The suit followed a contentious public hearing at which residents voiced opposition; the county has disputed the plaintiffs' characterization of the process in its formal response.

shortName: Dubose v. Cnty. of Imperial
citation: Tom Dubose et al vs. County of Imperial et al

shortName: In re Application of Ohio Power Co.
citation: In re Application of Ohio Power Co.
corporateEntities: AEP, Stargate manufacturing and data center site in Lordstown, OH  (Softbank, Oracle, OpenAI partnership), The Ohio Manufacturers' Association Energy Group, Ohio Power Co.,
summary: The Ohio Manufacturers' Association (OMA) is appealing to the Supreme Court of Ohio a Public Utilities Commission of Ohio (PUCO) decision approving a new tariff proposed by American Electric Power (AEP) Ohio specifically for data centers and other large-load customers. AEP's tariff requires data center customers to commit to minimum purchase requirements (paying for at least 85% of their stated power needs even if actual usage is lower), 12-year minimum contracts, and exit fees, which AEP says are needed to prevent stranded infrastructure costs from being shifted to other ratepayers; OMA's appeal argues the tariff is unlawfully discriminatory against a specific customer class, that PUCO improperly sanctioned AEP's earlier unilateral moratorium on new data center service requests, and that AEP's underlying demand projections were unsubstantiated. AEP counters that the tariff protects existing customers, including manufacturers, from bearing infrastructure costs caused by data centers.

shortName: Matter of Sierra Club v City of N. Tonawanda
citation: Matter of Sierra Club v City of N. Tonawanda
summary: This is a separate, related case from the PSC challenge above. The Sierra Club and three North Tonawanda residents petitioned to overturn the City of North Tonawanda Planning Board's local site plan approval allowing Digihost to install 14 shipping-container-sized structures housing cryptocurrency-mining computers on the grounds of the Fortistar power plant, alleging the Board violated the State Environmental Quality Review Act (SEQRA), the Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act, and local zoning and planning-review laws. State Supreme Court Justice Frank Sedita III dismissed the petition, ruling that the Sierra Club and residents — who alleged only that they lived "nearby" without specifying a distance or particularized harm — lacked standing, and that the petition was also untimely under the statutory filing deadline; the Fourth Department affirmed this dismissal.

shortName: Solar Energy Industries Association v. FERC
citation: Solar Energy Industries Assoc. v. FERC

shortName: Bluemile, Inc. v. Atlas Industrial Contractors, Ltd.
citation: Bluemile, Inc. v. Atlas Indus. Contrs., Ltd.
summary: Bluemile, Inc., a Columbus, Ohio data center operator, sued Atlas Industrial Contractors after an Atlas employee performing electrical work at Bluemile's data center caused a power surge on February 10, 2011 that disrupted Bluemile's computer networking services and allegedly caused lingering equipment damage; Atlas filed a separate but related action against Bluemile. A related coverage dispute arose when Bluemile sought business-interruption insurance benefits from Hartford Casualty Insurance Company, which contested the scope of recovery under Bluemile's policy. On appeal, the Ohio Tenth District Court of Appeals affirmed in part and reversed in part a trial court ruling that had granted Bluemile partial summary judgment against Hartford and granted Atlas judgment notwithstanding the verdict against Bluemile.

shortName: Riera Graterol v. Allison-Smith Co. LLC
citation: Perpetio Riera Graterol, Noris Azuaje Montilla, et al. v. Allison-Smith Company LLC

shortName: Burke v. Bd. of Cnty. Supervisors of Prince William Cnty.
citation: Katy Burke, et al. v. Board of County Supervisors of Prince William County
summary: The American Battlefield Trust and ten landowners near the Manassas National Battlefield — including Katy and Liam Burke, who keep horses and donkeys on their farm near the site — sued the Prince William County Board of County Supervisors and Digital Gateway developers (including GW Acquisition Co. and H&H Capital Acquisitions), alleging the Board's December 2023 approval of three rezoning ordinances permitting roughly 23 million square feet of data centers on 2,100+ acres was void from the outset because the county's public notice advertising for the December 2023 hearing violated Virginia Code § 15.2-2204(A) and the county's own zoning ordinance. The Prince William Circuit Court initially sustained the Board's demurrer to this claim, but on March 31, 2026, the Virginia Court of Appeals — deciding this case jointly with a related suit, Oak Valley Homeowners Ass'n v. Board of County Supervisors — ruled that the trial court had erred and held that the same advertising deficiencies rendered the rezonings void ab initio, reinforcing an earlier ruling in the Oak Valley case that had already halted the Digital Gateway project.

shortName: Masaitis v. Coreweave, Inc.
citation: Masaitis v. Coreweave, Inc.
summary: Lead plaintiff filed a putative securities class action against CoreWeave, Inc. and certain executives (CEO Michael Intrator, CFO Nitin Agrawal, and Chief Development Officer Brannin McBee), on behalf of investors who purchased CoreWeave stock between March 28, 2025 and December 15, 2025. The complaint alleges CoreWeave violated the Securities Exchange Act by overstating its ability to meet surging AI customer demand and materially understating the risk posed by its reliance on a single third-party data center supplier, Core Scientific — a risk that materialized when Core Scientific's shareholders rejected a planned all-stock merger with CoreWeave on October 30, 2025 (causing CoreWeave shares to fall more than 6%), and again in mid-December 2025 when further disclosures revealed weather-related construction delays at a Denton, Texas data center site and broader, earlier-known infrastructure setbacks. The suit seeks damages on behalf of the affected investor class under Sections 10(b) and 20(a) of the Securities Exchange Act.

shortName: Havron v. City of Bessemer
citation: Havron v. City of Bessemer
corporateEntities: Logistics Land Investment, LLC; Hyperscale "Project Marvel"
summary: David Havron and other Bessemer, Alabama-area property owners near Rock Mountain Lake sued the City of Bessemer over its rezoning process for "Project Marvel," a proposed $14.5 billion, 18-building hyperscale data center campus (later reported to involve developer Logistics Land Investment LLC and QTS Data Centers) on roughly 700 acres of forested land. Plaintiffs' original April 2025 complaint alleged the city failed to provide adequate public notice before a scheduled rezoning vote; after the city restarted its rezoning process and the council granted final approval in November 2025, plaintiffs amended their complaint to argue the rezoning constituted arbitrary and capricious "spot zoning" unsupported by a rational basis, inconsistent with surrounding land uses, unsupported by any comprehensive plan, and unjustified by public necessity. The case included a discovery dispute over a subpoena to the developer that was briefly appealed via a mandamus petition; the parties ultimately filed a joint stipulation of dismissal with prejudice on June 22, 2026, ending the litigation.

shortName: Preserve Our Yorkville & Community, LLC v. United City of Yorkville
citation: Preserve Our Yorkville & Community, LLC, Chuck Kasper, et al. v. The United City of Yorkville, Illinois, Pioneer Development LLC, and Yorkville Nexus V LLC

shortName: Seidel v. Atlas Power Holdings (ND), LLC
citation: Corey Seidel, et al. vs. Atlas Power Holdings (ND), LLC
summary: Twenty-two residents of Judson Township, North Dakota sued Atlas Power Holdings (operator of a Bitcoin-mining data center near Williston) and Williams County, alleging that persistent facility noise — measured by residents at 60 to 95+ decibels — constituted private and public nuisance and trespass, damaging their health, quality of life, and property values despite the installation of sound-mitigation walls. Plaintiffs also sought a writ of mandamus compelling Williams County to enforce its own zoning ordinance requiring that industrial noise and vibration be contained within the "Heavy Industrial" district, and asked the court to reverse what they alleged was an improper 2011 rezoning that permitted the facility's construction, along with at least $50,000 in damages. The court dismissed the trespass claim and both claims against Williams County in 2024, but let the nuisance and injunctive-relief claims against Atlas proceed; the parties reached a confidential settlement in mid-2025, with individual settlement agreements being finalized with residents into 2026.

shortName: Crosby v. Colleton Cnty.
citation: Miles Crosby, et al v. Colleton County
summary: Colleton County, South Carolina residents Miles Crosby and Jennifer Singleton, represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center, sued Colleton County to challenge a newly passed zoning ordinance allowing data centers to be built in rural areas of the county via a "special exception" permit. Plaintiffs allege the ordinance violates South Carolina zoning law, the county's own comprehensive plan, and its zoning code; the suit was filed shortly after developer Eagle Rock Partners applied under the new ordinance to build an 859-acre, 1,000-megawatt data center complex — potentially one of the largest in the country — within the ACE Basin, a 1.7-million-acre, largely undeveloped watershed around the Ashepoo, Combahee, and Edisto rivers. Plaintiffs argue the project would harm the area's rural character, dark night skies, water quality, and wildlife, and ask the court to invalidate the ordinance.

shortName: Caruthers v. Sangamon Cnty.
citation: Caruthers v. Sangamon County
summary: Herschel Caruthers II, Linda M. Caruthers, and several other Waverly, Illinois-area residents and a kennel business owner sued Sangamon County, the Sangamon County Board, and C1 Sangamon (an entity affiliated with data center developer CyrusOne) to overturn the county board's April 7, 2026 approval of a conditional use permit for a roughly 280-acre, four-building data center on agricultural land in Talkington Township. Plaintiffs allege, across five counts, that the approving resolution was misdated to obscure a procedural defect, that the county failed to adequately study the project's impacts (including noise affecting a neighboring farmstead), and that the county should have required rezoning rather than a conditional use permit for a project of this scale. The suit asks the court to declare the county's approval invalid and to enjoin the county from issuing related building permits.

shortName: Center for Biological Diversity v. City of Pittsburg
citation: Center for Biological Diversity v. City of Pittsburg
summary: The Center for Biological Diversity petitioned for a writ of mandate against the City of Pittsburg, California under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), challenging the City Council's November 4, 2024 certification of an environmental impact report and approval of the Pittsburg Technology Park Specific Plan — a 76.38-acre, three-phase development including a roughly 368,551-square-foot data center on former golf course land containing grassland and wetlands habitat. The Center alleged the EIR failed to adequately disclose or analyze greenhouse gas emissions, water supply and quality, wildfire, traffic, noise, and biological resource impacts, and failed to adopt feasible mitigation measures or consider reasonable alternatives. On December 11, 2025, the parties (the Center, the City, and real parties in interest Pittsburg Data Hub, LLC and AVAIO Digital Partners) agreed to a settlement incorporating enhanced mitigation measures — including a 100%-renewable-energy commitment, rooftop solar, EV charging infrastructure, recycled water for cooling, and a $750,000 developer payment to a climate-resiliency fund — and stayed the litigation pending compliance.

shortName: BladeRoom Group Ltd. v. Emerson Electric Co.
citation: BladeRoom Group Ltd. v. Emerson Electric Co.
summary: This is the appellate stage of the BladeRoom/Facebook/Emerson trade-secret dispute (previously summarized). After a jury found Emerson liable for breach of a non-disclosure agreement and willful and malicious misappropriation of BladeRoom's data center design trade secrets — awarding $10 million in lost profits and $20 million in unjust enrichment, later increased with punitive damages to roughly $60+ million — Emerson appealed to the Ninth Circuit. On August 30, 2021, the Ninth Circuit held that the district court misapplied English law in construing the NDA's two-year expiration clause, vacated the judgment, and remanded for a new trial to determine which disclosures occurred before versus after the NDA's termination date.

shortName: City of Sulphur Springs v. Luminant Mining Co., LLC
citation: City of Sulphur Springs vs. Luminant Mining Company, LLC, Luminant Generation Company, LLC, Vistra Corp., and Matthew Goering
summary: The City of Sulphur Springs sued former landowner Vistra Corp. and its subsidiaries Luminant Mining Company and Luminant Generation Company (along with an individual, Matthew Goering) over a deed restriction on land Vistra donated to the city in 2019 during its bankruptcy, which the city alleges was deceptively worded and now improperly bars the "commercial production, generation, or storage of electricity" needed to power a proposed 3,000-megawatt AI data center. The city contends Vistra falsely represented to regulators and the public that it held no rights over the land while secretly preserving the restriction to extract concessions once the data center project became viable. Vistra counter-sued, arguing the recorded land-use covenant is enforceable as written and that the city is trying to escape a bargain it accepted in 2019; the Texas Attorney General's Office has filed a brief supporting the city, arguing Luminant has used similar deed restrictions on other properties to entrench a potential energy monopoly.
