shortName: Doyle v. An Bord Pleanála
citation: Doyle & Ors v An Bord Pleanála & Ors
summary: Colin Doyle, Friends of the Irish Environment CLG, Futureproof Clare, Martin Knox, and Christine Sharp sought judicial review of two planning permissions granted by An Bord Pleanála (Ireland's national planning appeals board) in April 2024 for a large data center and substation development near Ennis, County Clare — comprising six two-story data halls (over 118,000 square meters) powered partly by 66 diesel generators and a 120MW gas facility, plus a new 110kV substation. Applicants raised six grounds for review, most concerning the development's climate impacts and alleged failure to comply with Ireland's Climate Action and Low Carbon Development Act, as well as a factual error in the Board's Environmental Impact Assessment regarding a Leisler's bat roost on the site (which the Board conceded was an error). On March 21, 2025, the High Court (Mr. Justice Richard Humphreys) dismissed the judicial review, finding the bat-related error was "harmless" and rejecting the broader climate and procedural grounds, thereby allowing the roughly €1.2 billion project to proceed.

shortName: Guido v. Columbia Cnty. Bd. of Comm'rs
citation: Gregory Guido, Jr. v. Columbia County Board Of Commissioners
corporateEntities: White Oak Business Center; Pumpkin Center
summary: Gregory Paul Guido Jr., a Harlem, Georgia resident, filed petitions for judicial review challenging the Columbia County Board of Commissioners' February 2026 approvals rezoning the White Oak Business Center and Pumpkin Center properties to Data Center District zoning for two large data center campuses. Guido alleges the county approved the rezonings without a verified water-usage or sewer-capacity analysis required by the county's Water and Sewer Division, relied on a stale traffic study prepared for an earlier version of the White Oak project, and failed to analyze the impacts of shifting the project's primary access point. The Superior Court dismissed all of Guido's related petitions (including a separate one concerning a nearby quarry) with prejudice; Guido moved for reconsideration, arguing the dismissal order failed to address the facts pled, improperly treated the distinct cases as one, and wrongly required land ownership (rather than proximity and demonstrable harm, which he argues is the correct standard under Georgia law) to establish standing. The matter is now before the Georgia Court of Appeals.

shortName: Beaver Ventures LLC v. Washington Cnty. Assessor
citation: Beaver Ventures LLC v. Washington County Assessor
summary: Beaver Ventures LLC — an entity affiliated with Digital Realty Trust — challenged the Washington County Assessor's denial of a property tax exemption sought for a Hillsboro, Oregon data center facility, reportedly valued at approximately $3.4 million in tax relief for the 2024–2025 tax year. A decision was issued in the matter; press coverage reports that Digital Realty's exemption request was rejected because the company had improperly attempted to combine two separate exemption applications into one filing.

shortName: Illinois Commerce Comm'n v. Commonwealth Edison Co.
citation: Illinois Commerce Commission On Its Own Motion v. Commonwealth Edison Company
corporateEntities: Commonwealth Edison Company; Illinois Commerce Commission; large-demand project applicants/customers, including data centers.
summary: This is a Commission-initiated regulatory investigation rather than adversarial litigation. Following its March 20, 2026 approval of revised ComEd tariffs allowing larger security deposits from "Large Demand Project Applicants or Customers" (LDPACs, i.e., data centers) to protect against costs from canceled or abandoned projects, the Illinois Commerce Commission opened a broader investigation — reflecting ComEd's disclosure that it has 75 pending large-load applications collectively requesting more than 28,000 megawatts, exceeding the utility's all-time peak demand of roughly 24,000 megawatts — into what additional protections, exemptions, or tariff modifications may be needed to shield existing ratepayers from the costs of connecting data centers to the grid. Consumer and environmental advocacy groups are participating in the proceeding and have urged the Commission to consider requiring data centers to bear the full cost of dedicated infrastructure and to adopt incentives for developers that bring their own new clean-energy generation.

shortName: Coresite, LLC v. Cnty. of Fairfax
citation: Coresite, LLC v. County of Fairfax
summary: CoreSite sued Fairfax County after the county's tax department repeatedly demanded that CoreSite disclose the identities and contact information of roughly 300 tenants at its four data centers and office building in Reston, Virginia, citing a Virginia Code provision allowing tax commissioners to require information relevant to assessing tax liability. CoreSite argues the county's demands were not reasonably specific to identifying Virginia taxpayers, were unduly burdensome, and risked exposing the company to liability from tenants whose contracts require confidentiality, since not all information requested was shown to relate to actual tax obligations. CoreSite asked the court to relieve it of the obligation to comply with the demands and to bar the county from taking adverse action — including threatened criminal penalties for noncompliance — while the dispute is resolved.

shortName: CyrusOne LLC v. City of Aurora
citation: CyrusOne LLC v. The City of Aurora, Illinois
summary: CyrusOne sued the City of Aurora, Illinois and telecommunications company Scientel Solutions LLC after Aurora approved a permit allowing Scientel to build a 195-foot communications tower near CyrusOne's data center campus (which hosts trading infrastructure for the Chicago Mercantile Exchange). CyrusOne, which had separately obtained a special use permit and variance in 2017 to build its own 350-foot tower for the same campus, alleged the Scientel tower would physically obstruct and interfere with wireless communications reaching CyrusOne's facility from the east and cause frequency congestion, and it sought a preliminary injunction to block Scientel's tower. The district court granted the defendants' motions to dismiss in part in July 2018 and later denied CyrusOne's preliminary injunction motion in March 2019; the parties ultimately settled the dispute through mediation, with the settlement terms undisclosed.

shortName: In re Frederick Cnty. Data Center Referendum Committee
citation: In re Frederick County Data Center Referendum Committee
summary: This matter arises from an appeal of a Frederick County, Maryland Circuit Court ruling against the Frederick County Data Center Referendum Committee (DCRC), a grassroots group that gathered more than 20,000 signatures seeking a public referendum to overturn Ordinance 26.01.001, which adopted a 2,600-acre "critical digital infrastructure" overlay zone for data center development. On June 18, 2026, Circuit Court Judge James A. Bonifant ruled that a county ordinance establishing a zoning map is not a "law" subject to referendum under the Frederick County Charter, and separately held the referendum petition itself was legally defective because its accompanying zoning maps were printed in black and white rather than the multi-color original, rendering them unreadable to voters. The DCRC announced it would appeal the ruling to the Supreme Court of Maryland, which is the proceeding reflected in this docket.

shortName: GW Acquisition Co., LLC v. Pageland Limited Liability Co.
citation: GW Acquisition Co., LLC v. Pageland Limited Liability Company
summary: GW Acquisition Co. (an affiliate of QTS Realty Trust) sued landowners Pageland Limited Liability Company and the Mitchell family for breach of contract, alleging they refused to honor purchase-and-sale agreements for roughly 175 acres that were part of GWA's larger, roughly 812-acre "Digital Gateway" data center assemblage in Prince William County, Virginia. GWA alleged the sellers wrongly refused to approve "proffers" needed for GWA's rezoning application and/or sought to terminate the agreements to obtain a higher price, jeopardizing the entire rezoning effort; GWA sought a preliminary injunction and damages, including recovery of legal costs it says it was owed from a related prior dispute with Pageland. The district court found GWA likely to succeed on the merits and that it would suffer irreparable harm without an injunction; Pageland appealed to the Fourth Circuit.

shortName: FLX Strong v. Town of Lansing Zoning Bd. of Appeals
citation: FLX Strong et al v. Town Of Lansing Zoning Board Of Appeals et al
corporateEntities: TeraWulf, Inc., Lake Hawkeye, LLC; Cuyahoga Operating Co., LLC
summary: FLX Strong and Cayuga Lake Environmental Action Now (CLEAN) filed an Article 78 petition against the Town of Lansing Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA) and developers TeraWulf Inc., its subsidiary Lake Hawkeye LLC, property owner Cayuga Operating Company, and an individual applicant, challenging the ZBA's December 22, 2025 decision (by a 3-2 vote) that a proposed data center at the former Cayuga Power Plant qualifies as a "general processing facility" — a permitted-by-right use under the town's Industrial Research zoning district — rather than requiring a more rigorous review process. Petitioners allege the ZBA's interpretation improperly stretched a legacy industrial zoning category to fit modern data center infrastructure, allowing the project to bypass environmental review, and that the proceedings were tainted by bias (citing the ZBA chairperson's private email expressing hope the project would be approved) and procedural irregularities, including a compressed 12-day review period. The petition asks the court to annul the ZBA's determination and remand for a new hearing excluding the chairperson; the matter was later appealed to the Appellate Division, Third Department.

shortName: King Sykes LLC v. City of Chicago
citation: King Sykes LLC v. The City of Chicago
summary: King Sykes LLC, owner of the vacant former Sykes Center site on Chicago's South Side, sued the City of Chicago and developer Scott Goodman, alleging the city and Goodman conspired to block a 2020–2021 deal to sell the 6.5-acre property to Equinix for $30 million to build a data center, in order to devalue the land so the city-Goodman "Bronzeville Lakefront" joint venture could later acquire it more cheaply. The complaint alleges city officials, including 4th Ward Alderwoman Sophia King, told Equinix the city would never approve a data center on the King Sykes site but would readily approve one on a nearby city-owned parcel (part of the former Michael Reese Hospital site) instead, causing Equinix to abandon its deal with King Sykes; the plaintiffs allege tortious interference with prospective economic advantage and sought $45 million in damages.

citation: Caparoula v. Board of County Supervisors of Prince William County
summary: William Caparoula and several neighboring property owners appealed the Prince William County Board of Supervisors' approval of Ordinance No. 23-52, which rezoned approximately 270 acres from a "Planned Mixed Residential" designation to a light-industrial district permitting data center use (the "Devlin" data center project), naming the Board and developer Stanley Martin Homes, LLC as appellees. Appellants argued the rezoning was arbitrary and capricious and constituted illegal spot zoning. On September 16, 2025, the Virginia Court of Appeals affirmed the rezoning, holding that the Board's decision met the "fairly debatable" standard, was not arbitrary and capricious, and did not constitute illegal spot zoning.

shortName: Blackboard Inc. v. International Business Machines Corp.
citation: Blackboard Inc. v. International Business Machines Corporation
summary: This federal case was a petition to vacate or modify an American Arbitration Association award, not a new lawsuit on the merits. Blackboard Inc. petitioned the court to vacate or modify in part an arbitration award that had found in IBM's favor on IBM's counterclaims arising from a professional services agreement governing data center operations and cloud migration — with the arbitration tribunal finding Blackboard had improperly withheld payment. In a June 2, 2022 Opinion and Order, the district court denied Blackboard's petition to vacate and confirmed the award in IBM's favor, entering judgment for $26,650,148 on one counterclaim and $3,143,101 on a second, plus interest, while denying IBM's request for attorney fees.

shortName: Haas v. Goochland Cnty.
citation: Haas, Cynthia v. Goochland County Of
summary: Four Goochland County, Virginia property owners — Cynthia Haas, Peggy Knisley, Virginia H. Reed, and Gail A. Minnick — sued Goochland County, its Board of Supervisors, and its Planning Commission, seeking to void the county's November 2025 approval (by a 4-1 vote) of a Technology Overlay District (TOD) and Technology Zone spanning about five miles along Route 288 in eastern Goochland, which would allow data centers and other high-tech uses near existing neighborhoods. Plaintiffs allege the county violated Virginia law governing zoning notice and process — including that the county's published notices were "wholly inadequate" and "confusingly defective," and that the version of the TOD ultimately adopted differed materially from what was described in the public notices, with late amendments introduced the night of the vote without further public input. The case remains in discovery over which of roughly 8,500 county documents must be produced; no trial date has been set.

shortName: Coll v. Hollenback Twp. Bd. of Supervisors
citation: Coll Craig A v. Hollenback Township Board Of Supervisors
summary: This appears to be part of a land-use dispute in Hollenback Township, where an attorney representing roughly 31 property owners seeking to rezone approximately 460 acres from residential to industrial (to permit data center development) took the matter to court after the township Board of Supervisors' February 22, 2026 hearing on the request was canceled amid disputes over whether the public had been properly notified, in potential violation of Pennsylvania's Sunshine Act. The docket number (filed March 24, 2026) falls shortly after this cancellation was reported.

shortName: In re Wisconsin Power & Light Co.
citation: Application of Wisconsin Power and Light Company for Approval of an Individual Contract Rate Service Agreement for a Large Load Customer in Beaver Dam, Dodge County, Wisconsin
corporateEntities: Meta, Alliant Energy, Wisconsin Power & Light
summary: This is a regulatory tariff proceeding rather than adversarial litigation. Alliant Energy (operating as Wisconsin Power and Light Company) applied to the Wisconsin Public Service Commission in April 2025 for approval of an Electric Service Agreement to serve a Meta data center in Beaver Dam, Wisconsin, under the utility's existing Individual Contract Rate tariff. Following a public comment period — extended after the Commission's administrative law judge ordered Alliant to refile the application with fewer redactions — the Commission approved a modified agreement on May 7, 2026, that strengthened termination-charge protections for existing customers, added reporting and financial-safeguard requirements, required the data center customer to contribute to state energy-efficiency programs, and directed Alliant to file a separate standardized large-load tariff for future data center customers.

shortName: Data Foundry, Inc. v. City of Austin
citation: Data Foundry, Inc. v. City of Austin
summary: Data Foundry, Inc., an internet service provider operating data centers in Austin, sued the City of Austin over rates charged by Austin Energy, the city-owned electric utility, alleging the rates are unjust, unreasonable, excessive, confiscatory, discriminatory, and constitute a taking. The trial court dismissed Data Foundry's claims for lack of standing; the Fourteenth Court of Appeals held Data Foundry had standing but still affirmed dismissal of the claims on other grounds. On April 9, 2021, the Texas Supreme Court held that Data Foundry has standing as a ratepayer to challenge generally applicable municipal utility rates without needing to show an injury distinct from other ratepayers, reversed the courts below in part, and remanded the case to the trial court for further proceedings on the merits of the rate challenge.

shortName: Intergate Quincy II LLC v. Grant Cnty.
citation: Intergate Quincy II LLC et al v. Grant County
summary: Intergate Quincy (a Sabey Data Centers entity) sued Grant County, Washington over property tax assessments on its Quincy data center campus, alleging the county assessor overvalued the property — assessing it at $239 million in 2020 and $237 million in 2021, versus the roughly $132 million and $123 million the company contends the property was actually worth. Intergate Quincy states it paid approximately $3.3 million in county taxes under protest over the relevant period, representing nearly $2 million it now seeks refunded as excess charges resulting from the allegedly inflated valuation. This was not the first such dispute in Grant County — the county was previously sued by another data center operator, H5 Data Centers, over a similarly contested assessment in 2019.

shortName: McDavid v. Scioto Cnty. Bd. of Cnty. Comm'rs
citation: McDavid, Patrick v. Scioto County Board Of County Commissioners
corporateEntities: Project Dazzler; Tilted Gate, LLC; Google
summary: Scioto County, Ohio resident Patrick McDavid sued the Scioto County Board of County Commissioners, alleging violations of Ohio's Open Meetings Act ("Sunshine Law") in connection with the board's negotiation of a Community Reinvestment Area tax agreement tied to a proposed Google data center campus. McDavid alleges the commissioners improperly conducted public business in closed-door executive sessions and failed to comply with state transparency requirements during the negotiations; the suit seeks a court order enforcing compliance with the statute and potentially invalidating actions taken in the allegedly improper sessions. This case is separate from Project Dazzler, a different $1 billion data center proposal also underway in Scioto County.

citation: Sharp v. City of Wilmington, Ohio

shortName: Eagan Capital, LLC v. City of Eagan
citation: Eagan Capital, LLC v. City of Eagan
summary: Eagan Capital, LLC, a data center owner, sued the City of Eagan, Minnesota after the city council adopted a one-year moratorium in February 2026 on new or expanded data center development involving more than 20 megawatts of electricity use within 500 feet of homes. Eagan Capital argues the city lacks legal authority to regulate electricity demand or impose the moratorium, contending that the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission has exclusive authority over electricity regulation in the state; the company seeks $50,000 in damages. The city has said it denied a related Interim Use Permit to Eagan Capital after finding the company had installed temporary chiller units without required permits, and states it intends to defend the moratorium.

shortName: Blocktree Properties, LLC v. Public Utility District No. 2 of Grant Cnty. Washington
citation: Blocktree Properties, LLC v. Public Utility District No. 2 of Grant County Washington
summary: Blocktree Properties and several affiliated Bitcoin-mining/data-hosting LLCs and an individual sued Grant County's Public Utility District No. 2 and its commissioners, alleging the utility's rate structure for cryptocurrency-mining customers violated Washington ratemaking law and the Due Process and Privileges and Immunities Clauses of the Washington State Constitution. Plaintiffs, who operated mining facilities drawn to the district by its low-cost hydroelectric power, sought declaratory and injunctive relief and damages; the court denied a preliminary injunction in 2019 (affirmed by the Ninth Circuit on interlocutory appeal), and on March 12, 2020, granted summary judgment in the utility district's favor on all claims, closing the case.

shortName: Columbia Riverkeeper v. FERC
citation: Columbia Riverkeeper’s request for rehearing of order issuing original license and request for stay
summary: Columbia Riverkeeper petitioned the Ninth Circuit to review the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission's issuance of an original hydroelectric license for the Goldendale pumped-storage energy project in Washington State, which would be built partly on Pushpum, a site sacred to the Yakama Nation, near the John Day Dam on the Columbia River. Columbia Riverkeeper argues the project — reported to be a major prospective power source for a nearby hyperscale data center campus proposed by STACK Infrastructure — will cause significant and unavoidable adverse impacts to Yakama cultural and historic resources, as separately found in a state environmental review; the Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation filed a related, separate petition for review of the same FERC licensing decision.

shortName: Citizens for Faquier Cnty. v. Town of Warrenton
citation: Citizens for Fauquier County v. Town of Warrenton, Virginia, et al
summary: Citizens for Fauquier County, a conservation nonprofit, sued the Town of Warrenton in Fauquier County Circuit Court in December 2022 to compel disclosure of more than 3,100 emails concerning Amazon's proposal to build a 220,000-square-foot data center in the town, after the Town withheld the records under the Virginia Freedom of Information Act's "working papers" exemption for the mayor and town manager. The circuit court ruled the records could be withheld; the nonprofit appealed, and on July 30, 2024, the Virginia Court of Appeals reversed, holding the trial court had misapplied the "or" in the statutory exemption to shield both officials' correspondence.

shortName: Digital 60 & 80 Merritt, LLC v. Bd. of Assessment Appeals
citation: Digital 60 & 80 Merritt, LLC v. Bd. of Assessment Appeals
summary: Digital 60 & 80 Merritt, LLC, owner of a data center property at 60 Merritt Boulevard in Trumbull, Connecticut, brought a real estate tax appeal challenging the Town of Trumbull's property tax assessment, which the plaintiff alleged was grossly excessive (the town valued the property at roughly $15.2 million after Digital had purchased it for $45,000, and further imposed a 25% penalty for an allegedly late personal-property declaration). The trial court sustained Digital's appeals and ordered a reduction in the assessment, applying an income-capitalization approach to determine fair market value; the Town and its Board of Assessment Appeals appealed, arguing the trial court's valuation findings were clearly erroneous. The Appellate Court of Connecticut affirmed the trial court's judgment reducing the assessment.

shortName: Data Foundry, Inc. v. City of Austin
citation: Data Foundry, Inc. v. City of Austin
summary: Data Foundry, Inc., an internet service provider operating data centers in Austin, sued the City of Austin over rates charged by Austin Energy, the city-owned electric utility, alleging the rates are unjust, unreasonable, excessive, confiscatory, discriminatory, and constitute a taking. The trial court dismissed Data Foundry's claims for lack of standing; the Fourteenth Court of Appeals held Data Foundry had standing but still affirmed dismissal of the claims on other grounds. On April 9, 2021, the Texas Supreme Court held that Data Foundry has standing as a ratepayer to challenge generally applicable municipal utility rates without needing to show an injury distinct from other ratepayers, reversed the courts below in part, and remanded the case to the trial court for further proceedings on the merits of the rate challenge.

shortName: Decatur Twp. Civic Council Inc. v. Indianapolis Metropolitan Development Comm'n
citation: Decatur Township Civic Council Inc., Timothy W. McWhirter, Trustee, Janice F. McWhirter, Trustee et al v. Indianapolis Metropolitan Development Commission, City-County Council of Indianapolis, Marion County, Indiana, Sabey Data Center Properties LLC et al
summary: The Decatur Township Civic Council and several individual property owners petitioned for judicial review of the Indianapolis Metropolitan Development Commission's March 18, 2026 decision granting a "variance of use" allowing Sabey Data Center Properties LLC to build a roughly $4 billion, 130-acre, 250-megawatt data center campus. Petitioners allege the Commission and City-County Council approved the variance and related commitment modifications in violation of Indiana law and petitioners' due process rights, contending Sabey used a variance to bypass the formal rezoning process — which would have let the district's City-County Council representative "call down" the matter for a full council vote — and that the project conflicts with the area's approved mixed-use plan. The petition seeks to overturn the approval and, separately, requests an injunction to block construction while the case proceeds.

shortName: In re NorthWestern Energy's Provision of Electricity Supply Service to Data Centers
citation: In Re NorthWestern Energy's Provision of Electricity Supply Service to Data Centers
summary: Earthjustice, on behalf of a coalition of conservation, Indigenous, senior-citizen, faith, and social-justice organizations, filed a complaint with the Montana Public Service Commission (PSC) alleging that NorthWestern Energy — the state's largest utility — is unlawfully planning to begin supplying electricity (reportedly up to 1,400 megawatts under signed letters of intent with three data center developers) before the PSC has determined, as Montana law requires, that doing so will not adversely impact NorthWestern's more than 413,000 existing residential customers. The complaint alleges NorthWestern has "stonewalled" the PSC's own requests for information about the data center agreements and improperly delayed seeking regulatory review until after contracts are executed, and asks the Commission to investigate NorthWestern's conduct and require greater transparency, including disclosure of the identities of data center applicants and the costs of any related transmission studies.

shortName: Soriano v. City of Hobart Plan Comm'n
citation: Angelita Soriano, Joseph Conn, Barbara Koteleset al v. City of Hobart Plan Commission, Common Council of the City of Hobart, Indiana
summary: Angelita Soriano and several other Hobart, Indiana residents sued the City of Hobart Plan Commission and the Hobart Common Council in Lake Superior Court, alleging the city violated their due process rights under the U.S. and Indiana constitutions when it rezoned roughly 725 acres of residential land to light-industrial use to accommodate a proposed Amazon data center. Plaintiffs contend the city's actions — including limiting public comment until after votes were taken — were "arbitrary, capricious," and unsupported by substantial evidence, and argue the project will diminish their property values and use and enjoyment of their homes. The suit asks the court to vacate the challenged rezoning resolutions and related land-transfer actions.

shortName: Thornton v. City of Kuna
citation: Layne Thornton, et. al. v. The City of Kuna
summary: Layne Thornton and two Toledo Dairy business entities, whose farmland borders the proposed 620-acre "Gemstone Technology Park" data center site, filed a petition for judicial review challenging the Kuna City Council's April 2025 approval (by a 3-2 vote, with the mayor breaking the tie) of the project's rezoning. Petitioners alleged that council member Greg McPherson should have recused himself from the vote because he was employed by Thornton, creating an economic conflict of interest, and cited concerns about the project's traffic, power, water use, and environmental impact, including testimony that the data center's electricity demand could raise local power rates. The district court rejected the petition, finding Thornton had not shown a direct, particularized economic interest distinguishable from the broader community's interest in the project, and specifically held that potential power-rate increases were not a sufficiently direct impact; the petitioners have appealed that dismissal to the Idaho Supreme Court.

shortName: BladeRoom Group Ltd. v. Facebook, Inc.
citation: BladeRoom Group Limited v. Facebook, Inc.
summary: BladeRoom Group and an affiliate sued Facebook, Emerson Electric, and related Emerson entities in 2015, alleging that after BladeRoom pitched its modular data center design to Facebook under a non-disclosure agreement in 2011–2012, Facebook and Emerson conspired to misappropriate BladeRoom's trade secrets to build Facebook's Luleå, Sweden data center, and that Facebook then shared the design through the Open Compute Project without authorization. BladeRoom's claims included breach of the NDA, misappropriation of trade secrets, unjust enrichment, and unfair competition, and it originally sought roughly $365 million in damages. Facebook settled with BladeRoom during trial for a reported $365 million; the case proceeded to a jury verdict against Emerson alone, which found willful and malicious trade secret misappropriation and breach of contract and awarded roughly $30 million in compensatory damages (later increased with exemplary damages and prejudgment interest to over $77 million) — a judgment the Ninth Circuit later vacated in part on appeal, remanding for further proceedings regarding the NDA's expiration date.

shortName: Kentucky Industrial Alliance, LLC v. City of Cave City
citation: Kentucky Industrial Alliance, LLC v. City of Cave City
summary: Kentucky Industrial Alliance (KIA), developer of a proposed $4.8 billion, 600-acre, 1.2-gigawatt AI data center campus near Mammoth Cave National Park, sued the City of Cave City, its council, and the Joint City-County Planning Commission after the city adopted a 12-month moratorium on data center applications in May 2026 — shortly after KIA had submitted development plans. KIA alleges the moratorium was enacted specifically to block its already-pending project and unlawfully halted development after it had invested more than $2 million assembling and preparing the land, and separately alleges the Planning Commission failed to process its development plan application. The city disputes that KIA ever submitted a valid application (calling it only a "two-page" filing) and argues KIA lacks standing and has no vested rights; a hearing on KIA's request for a preliminary injunction against the moratorium was held July 20, 2026, and this case has since been consolidated with a related suit (below) challenging the underlying annexation of the property.

shortName: 1778 Rich Pike LLC v. Clifton Twp. Zoning
citation: 1778 Rich Pike LLC vs. Clifton Twp Pa Zoning
summary:
1778 Rich Pike LLC appealed the Clifton Township Zoning Hearing Board's November 19, 2025 decision to the Lackawanna County Court of Common Pleas. The Board had denied the developer's substantive validity challenge to the township's zoning ordinance, which the developer argued excluded data center uses. The appeal contends that data center uses are legitimate land uses entitled to zoning accommodation under state law, that the ordinance fails to define or classify data center uses and is therefore exclusionary, that the ordinance lacks any comparable use to which data centers could be analogized, and that it provides no reasonable path to approval by special exception.

shortName: In re Evergy Kansas Metro, Inc.
citation: In the Matter of the Application of Evergy Kansas Metro, Inc., Evergy Kansas South, Inc., and Evergy Kansas Central, Inc. for Approval of Large Load Service Rate Plan and Associated Tariffs
summary: This is a regulatory rate proceeding rather than adversarial litigation. Evergy applied to the Kansas Corporation Commission (KCC) in February 2025 for approval of a new Large Load Power Service (LLPS) rate plan designed for electric customers — primarily data centers and large manufacturers — requiring 75 megawatts or more of peak power, in order to recover the incremental cost of serving such customers without shifting those costs to existing ratepayers. On November 6, 2025, the KCC approved a unanimous settlement reached among Evergy, KCC Staff, the Citizens' Utility Ratepayer Board, industrial-consumer and data-center industry groups (including Google and the Data Center Coalition), and conservation organizations (including the Sierra Club), establishing minimum contract terms of 12 to 17 years (with up to a five-year ramp-up period), direct assignment of large-load-specific system upgrade costs to the new customer, and incentives for large-load customers that help fund or generate their own clean energy.

shortName: Franklin Citizens for Responsible Development, Inc. v. City of Franklin Planning & Zoning Comm'n
citation: Franklin Citizens for Responsible Development, Inc. v. City of Franklin Planning and Zoning Commission, et al.
corporateEntities: Tenkey Landco I, LLC; SPDJ Partners, LLC; OTN Development Company, LLC; “Project Lionsgate/Blackjack”
summary: Franklin Citizens for Responsible Development, a local nonprofit, sued the City of Franklin Planning and Zoning Commission and developer entities (Tenkey Landco I, LLC, SPDJ Partners, LLC, and OTN Development Company, LLC) behind a proposed AI data center campus with on-site power generation on roughly 200 acres near I-65 (referred to as "Project Lionsgate/Blackjack"). Plaintiffs allege the Commission's March 2026 unanimous approval of a preliminary development plan for the project was arbitrary, capricious, and inconsistent with the City of Franklin Zoning Ordinance, because the Commission had previously rejected a proposed zoning text amendment that would have explicitly allowed data centers and on-site power generation, and had indicated any such project would instead require a conditional-use permit — which only the Franklin Board of Adjustments can grant. The suit also raises concerns about noise, light pollution, air emissions, and strain on local water resources, and asks the court to overturn the preliminary plan approval. This is the second of two related lawsuits over the project; in the other, the developer (TenKey) is separately suing Simpson County over a conditional-use-permit ordinance the company says gives the county excessive control over the project.

shortName: Concerned Citizens of Spartanburg Cnty. v. Valara Holdings, LLC
citation: Concerned Citizens of Spartanburg Cnty. v. Valara Holdings, LLC
summary: Concerned Citizens of Spartanburg County, represented by the South Carolina Environmental Law Center, sued Valara Holdings LLC and Spartanburg County, alleging that a roughly $2.8–3 billion data center project on the former Kohler industrial site was improperly classified and approved as a "minor land development" under the county's Unified Land Management Ordinance — a designation that bypassed the public review process (planning commission review, public notice, hearings, and a public vote) required for "major" developments. Plaintiffs contend the developer split the project into two applications to keep each under the minor-development threshold, despite the combined project's scale, and point to a much smaller industrial facility that was separately classified as "major," while raising concerns about water quality, air emissions from an associated natural gas power plant, and the ordinance's protective purpose. The suit asks the court to require the county to conduct the major-development public review process; a hearing was scheduled for July 30, 2026.

shortName: Piatt v. City of Granbury
citation: Daniel Piatt, et al v. City of Granbury et al
summary: Daniel Piatt and other Granbury, Texas residents sued the City of Granbury and city officials after the city council voted April 7, 2026 to rezone a 2,100-acre parcel ("Knox Ranch") backed by Bilateral Energy for a potential data center project known as "Project Patriot." Plaintiffs allege the annexation of the land, completed in January 2026, was marked by procedural violations, including that officials failed to properly disclose the annexation's connection to the data center plans, and that city officials violated the Texas Open Meetings Act by deliberately staggering their arrival times during a tour of a Bilateral Energy facility in Dallas to avoid triggering the Act's quorum and public-notice requirements (an alleged "walking quorum"). The suit seeks a pause on further action related to the data center, revocation of the annexation, and damages.

shortName: Guido v. Columbia Cnty. Bd. of Comm'rs
citation: Gregory Guido, Jr. v. Columbia County Board Of Commissioners
corporateEntities: White Oak Business Center; Pumpkin Center
summary: Gregory Paul Guido Jr., a Harlem, Georgia resident, filed petitions for judicial review challenging the Columbia County Board of Commissioners' February 2026 approvals rezoning the White Oak Business Center and Pumpkin Center properties to Data Center District zoning for two large data center campuses. Guido alleges the county approved the rezonings without a verified water-usage or sewer-capacity analysis required by the county's Water and Sewer Division, relied on a stale traffic study prepared for an earlier version of the White Oak project, and failed to analyze the impacts of shifting the project's primary access point. The Superior Court dismissed all of Guido's related petitions (including a separate one concerning a nearby quarry) with prejudice; Guido moved for reconsideration, arguing the dismissal order failed to address the facts pled, improperly treated the distinct cases as one, and wrongly required land ownership (rather than proximity and demonstrable harm, which he argues is the correct standard under Georgia law) to establish standing. The matter is now before the Georgia Court of Appeals.

shortName: Kentucky Industrial Alliance, LLC v. City of Cave City, the Cave City Council and the Joint City-County Planning Commission
citation: Kentucky Industrial Alliance, LLC v. City of Cave City, the Cave City Council and the Joint City-County Planning Commission
summary: In a second, related lawsuit, Kentucky Industrial Alliance (KIA) asked the Barren County Circuit Court to void Cave City's September 2024 annexation (Ordinance 24-9-9C) of the approximately 245-acre former Branstetter property where KIA's data center project is planned — arguing that if the annexation is invalid, the property would fall outside city jurisdiction and the city's data center moratorium (challenged in the companion case above) would not apply to it. KIA's complaint centers on a roughly 0.09-acre parcel containing the historic Shaw Cemetery within the annexed tract, alleging that Branstetter Family Holdings did not actually own the cemetery parcel (whose title traces to a 1902 deed) when it signed consent to the annexation, and that KIA — not Branstetter — was declared the cemetery's rightful successor-in-title by a December 2024 default judgment in unrelated litigation; KIA contends the entire annexation ordinance must be invalidated, rather than just the cemetery parcel excised from it, because the city intended to annex one unified site. This case has been consolidated with KIA's earlier moratorium challenge, with the annexation issue proceeding first since it could resolve the city's jurisdiction over the property entirely.

citation: Citizens for Fauquier County v. Town of Warrenton, Virginia, et al
summary: Citizens for Fauquier County and ten individual plaintiffs separately sued the Warrenton Town Council (later joined by Amazon Data Services as an intervenor) to overturn the Council's February 2023 special-use-permit approval for the same Amazon data center. Plaintiffs contend the Town's April 2021 zoning amendment permitting data centers was void from its enactment because the Council's initiating resolution failed to state a statutorily required purpose, and that any permits issued under the amendment — including Amazon's — should be voided as a result.

shortName: In re Appalachian Power Co.
citation: Appalachian Power Company and Wheeling Power Company
summary: This is a regulatory rate proceeding, not adversarial litigation: Appalachian Power Company and Wheeling Power Company applied to the West Virginia Public Service Commission to establish tariff terms for "large-load" customers such as data centers, with Google participating as an intervenor. After negotiation, Appalachian Power, Google, and a group representing West Virginia manufacturers reached a settlement — later subject to Commission approval — setting minimum contract terms for large-load customers, including a 100 MW minimum capacity per site, a minimum 12-year initial contract term, and a requirement to commit to purchasing at least 80% of expected power consumption.

shortName: Greenidge Generation LLC v. New York State Dep't of Environmental Conservation
citation: Greenidge Generation LLC vs. New York State Department of Environmental Conservation et al
summary: Greenidge Generation, operator of a natural gas power plant and Bitcoin-mining data center in Dresden, New York, sued the state Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) after DEC denied renewal of the facility's Clean Air Act Title V operating permit, and later moved to force the plant's closure. Greenidge alleged DEC lacked authority under New York's Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA) to deny the permit based on a determination that continued operation would be inconsistent with statewide greenhouse-gas limits, and that DEC misapplied the CLCPA by failing to assess whether a justification or mitigation measures existed for the denial. On November 14, 2024, the Yates County Supreme Court annulled DEC's permit denial, holding that while the CLCPA authorizes such denials, the agency's discretion is limited and must rest on proper analysis; DEC appealed, but the parties later settled, with DEC agreeing to issue Greenidge a new five-year Title V permit incorporating emissions reductions, and the appeal was discontinued by stipulation in late 2025.

shortName: Georgia Interfaith Power & Light v. Georgia Public Service Comm'n
citation: Georgia Interfaith Power & Light, Park Avenue Baptist Church, Unitarian Universalist Church of Savannah, Sierra Club, Adrien Webber, in his capacity individually and as member of Sierra Club, Southern Alliance for Clean Energy VS. Georgia Public Service Commission
summary: Georgia Interfaith Power & Light, Park Avenue Baptist Church, the Unitarian Universalist Church of Savannah, the Sierra Club (and its Georgia Chapter Director Adrien Webber, individually), and the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy — represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center and Sierra Club — petitioned the Fulton County Superior Court to review the Georgia Public Service Commission's December 2025 decision approving Georgia Power's plan to add roughly 10 gigawatts of new electric generation, including expensive new gas units at Plant McIntosh, largely to serve anticipated data center demand. Petitioners allege the Commission violated Georgia law by approving the buildout without properly demonstrating the new capacity is actually needed — noting that some of the demand is speculative and tied to data centers that have not signed contracts with Georgia Power — and argue the decision will leave "captive" ratepayers responsible for an estimated $50–60 billion in costs over coming decades. The petition asks the court to send the approval back to the Commission for reconsideration.

shortName: Cresa Global Inc. v. Chirisa Capital Management (US) LLC
citation: Cresa Global Inc. et al. v. Chirisa Capital Management (US) LLC et al
summary: Cresa Global Inc. and Site Selection Group, LLC sued Chirisa Capital Management (US) LLC and Chirisa Richmond LLC, alleging they procured CoreWeave, Inc. as a client that ultimately entered into a Master Services Agreement with the Chirisa defendants to license their Virginia data center, and that they are owed a transaction commission for their brokering efforts despite having no formal written agreement with the defendants. Plaintiffs pled breach of contract or, alternatively, unjust enrichment or quantum meruit; a substantially similar suit the plaintiffs had filed in New York was dismissed in 2024. On January 9, 2025, the Delaware Superior Court denied the defendants' motion to dismiss on forum non conveniens grounds, holding that Delaware — the state of incorporation for both defendant entities — had a sufficient interest in the dispute and that the defendants had not shown the burden of Delaware litigation outweighed Delaware's interest.

shortName: Milwaukee Riverkeeper, Inc. v. City of Racine
citation: Milwaukee Riverkeeper, Inc. vs. City of Racine et al
summary: Milwaukee Riverkeeper and Midwest Environmental Advocates sued the City of Racine to force release of public records showing the projected water use of the first phase of Microsoft's data center campus in Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin, after the city withheld or redacted the figures in response to an open-records request. The lawsuit was resolved quickly: the city released the requested information — showing the first phase of the Microsoft campus was projected to use approximately 8 million gallons of water annually — within about two days of the suit being filed, prompting its closure.

shortName: Hatfield v. U.S. Army Corps of Engineers
citation: Hatfield v. U.S. Army Corps of Engineers
summary: Ten southern West Virginia residents sued the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, and project developer TransGas Development Systems over the proposed Adams Fork Energy project — a 117-engine, self-contained "micro-grid" power plant and ammonia facility intended to include associated data centers near Wharncliffe on the Mingo-Logan county line. Plaintiffs allege the project would violate the Endangered Species Act (threatening the endangered Guyandotte Crayfish, threatened Big Sandy Crayfish, and endangered Gray Bat and Northern long-eared bat), the Clean Water Act, the National Environmental Policy Act, and the Natural Gas Act, because the federal defendants have not conducted required environmental consultation, review, or permitting despite the state having already issued an air-emissions construction permit for what plaintiffs say is legally a "major source" of air pollution. Plaintiffs sought a temporary restraining order and preliminary and permanent injunctions barring further construction activity until all required federal reviews are completed.

shortName: In re Ohio Power Co.
citation: In the Matter of the Application of Ohio Power Company for New Tariffs Related to Data Centers and Mobile Data Centers
summary: American Electric Power (AEP) Ohio applied to the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio (PUCO) for a new tariff specifically governing data centers and other large-load customers, after AEP reported more than 50 data centers in its interconnection queue representing over 30,000 megawatts of additional demand and had paused new data center service requests in 2023 pending a framework. In July 2025, the PUCO approved a negotiated version of AEP's proposed tariff requiring data center customers to pay for at least 85% of their stated power needs regardless of actual usage, sign minimum 12-year contracts, and pay exit fees equal to three years of minimum charges if they leave early — terms AEP says are needed to prevent stranded infrastructure costs from falling on other ratepayers. The Ohio Manufacturers' Association has separately appealed this approval (and PUCO's earlier sanctioning of AEP's data-center service moratorium) to the Ohio Supreme Court, arguing the tariff unlawfully discriminates against a specific customer class.

shortName: City of Imperial v. Cnty. of Imperial
citation: City of Imperial vs. County of Imperial et al
summary: The City of Imperial sued Imperial County and its Board of Supervisors, along with developer Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing, LLC and Dubose Design Group, Inc., over the county's approval of a nearly 1-million-square-foot AI data center complex at Aten and Clark roads. The city alleges the county improperly classified a required grading permit as "ministerial" — an administrative act requiring no discretionary review — to bypass the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), and contends the project instead required rezoning and a conditional use permit given its scale. The city sought an immediate injunction halting grading and construction pending resolution; in February 2026 the court ruled the city's amended complaint did not, as pleaded, state a legally sufficient cause of action.

shortName: FX Solutions v. Broad Reach Power, LLC
citation: FX Solutions v. Encap., et al.
corporateEntities: FX Solutions; Encap; Quantica; Broad Reach Power; Engie
summary: FX Solutions and its principal, Montana businessman Rick Tabish, sued Broad Reach Power, LLC, its Texas private-equity owner EnCap, and successor entity Quantica Infrastructure, alleging breach of contract, breach of the covenant of good faith and fair dealing, tortious interference, and unjust enrichment arising from a soured deal involving land near a NorthWestern Energy substation in Broadview, Montana. FX alleges it sold 350 acres surrounding the substation to Broad Reach Power in reliance on a promise that Broad Reach would supply power (at roughly $24 per megawatt-hour, well below market rates) to run FX's planned data center, but that Broad Reach — secretly directed by EnCap — never intended to deliver the power and instead transferred its energy assets to the newly formed Quantica, which is now building its own data center on the land FX sold, using a separate agreement with NorthWestern for up to 1 gigawatt of power. The defendants deny any binding power-purchase contract existed, characterizing the arrangement as an unenforceable "agreement to agree," and argue Broad Reach Power has since been dissolved; FX seeks unspecified damages.

shortName: Great Lakes Neighbors, Inc. v. City of Port Washington Joint Review Bd.
citation: Great Lakes Neighbors, Inc. v. City of Port Washington Joint Review Board et al
corporateEntities: Vantage Data Center "Lighthouse"; Open AI; Oracle
summary: Great Lakes Neighbors Inc. sued the City of Port Washington and its Joint Review Board, seeking to void a $458 million tax incremental financing (TIF) district the city approved in November 2025 to fund infrastructure for Vantage Data Center's "Lighthouse" campus (part of the OpenAI/Oracle "Stargate" program). The suit alleges the district fails Wisconsin's statutory requirements — that at least half the property be blighted or qualify as industrial land, and that the project pass the "but-for" test showing it would not proceed without TIF support — and further alleges the city improperly agreed to reimburse the developer for costs (including interest payments) not allowed under the TIF statute, and that officials may have violated the state's Open Meetings law during related discussions. The suit asks the court to declare the TIF district invalid.
